Hardest calls:
1. aru/nai counted as one set (same verb, only negated). Kept the higher-count shape: jikan ga nai (1664) over jikan ga aru (725), hima ga nai, yoyuu ga nai. Kept the aru shape for kyoumi, jishin, keiken, yotei and sainou. ii/warui pairs are different adjectives, so both stayed where both are common (kimochi, kibun, choushi, un, tsugou).
2. The noun + suru line. I used the particles column: where the form with no particle dominates, it is a plain suru verb and I cut it. That cut jama (917 of 1342 have no particle), shitsumon, kenka, henji, nakanaori, yakedo and keshou, even with big counts. Kept hanashi o suru (o in 2821 of 3600, and the 'X no hanashi' trap) and kega o suru (current list, 'get hurt' trap), both borderline. Also kept the sets where suru stands for wear or play: masuku o suru, kakkou o suru, geemu o suru, sakkaa o suru.
3. ki- sets. Kept ki ni iru, ki ga tsuku and ki o tsukau, which work like single verbs and are in the current list. Left ki ga kawaru, ki ga chiru and ki ga noranai for the idiom list. The idiom pass should check all six.

Hardest calls:
1. Where the idiom list starts. ki ni iru, ki ga tsuku and ki o tsukau are lexicalized ki-expressions, close to the out-of-scope example ki ga au. I kept them because they are among the most common sets of all, their siblings are already in the versatility list, and idiom-candidates.json does not include them, so cutting them here would drop them from both lists. osewa ni naru (kept, and gochisou ni naru beside it) is also in idiom-candidates.json. The idiom pass should drop it there.
2. The noun + suru boundary. I cut verbal-noun + suru sets (shitsumon o suru, kenka o suru, jama o suru, henji o suru, sewa o suru, iiwake o suru, keshou o suru, shukudai o suru) as plain suru verbs. I kept sets where suru means something other than "do the noun": kega o suru (get hurt), masuku o suru and tokei o suru (wear), geemu o suru and sakkaa o suru (play). I also kept hanashi o suru, the most frequent candidate. hanashi is not a verbal noun, and X no hanashi (o) suru is how people say "talk about X". It is the call most open to challenge.
3. Correcting the film corpus. I swapped kuruma o tomeru (240, mostly the film line "stop the car") for shuuden ga nakunaru. I lifted sets with low or no counts that Japanese people say every day: warikan ni suru, konbini ni yoru, kasa o sasu, densha ni maniau, okane o orosu, mezamashi o kakeru, sentakumono o hosu, nimotsu ga todoku, kafun ga tobu, taifuu ga kuru, juuden ga kireru, gohan ga dekiru, gochisou ni naru, kata ga koru, chiketto o toru. I dropped film-plot sets with high counts: keisatsu o yobu, mondai o kakaeru, koi ni ochiru, shigoto ni modoru, sekinin o toru, ishiki o ushinau.
4. Pairs and near-duplicates. Where the second member of a pair is not clearly as common, I kept one and left the other as a partner note:
   - jikan ga nai over jikan ga aru
   - kyoumi ga aru over kyoumi ga nai
   - mise ga aku over mise ga shimaru
   - se ga takai over se ga hikui
   - kaigi ga aru over kaigi ni deru
   - shiai ni katsu over shiai ni makeru
   - kaze ga utsuru over kaze o utsusu
   - masuku o suru over masuku o tsukeru
   - masuku o hazusu over megane o hazusu
   - uchi o deru over ie o deru
   - youji ga aru over you ga aru
   - meeru o okuru over messeeji o okuru, to match meeru ga kuru and meeru o kaesu
   - densha ni maniau over jikan ni maniau
   - denwa ga kakaru over denwa ga kakatte kuru (the same set in another shape)
   I kept onaka ga suku and onaka ga heru as different words, and kept both netsu ga aru and netsu ga deru.
5. Free combinations. I kept guessable but typical sets that people say constantly (doa o akeru, hon o yomu, gohan o taberu, uchi ni kaeru, toire ni iku, kaimono ni iku, kodomo ga iru). I limited X o nomu to osake and koohii, plus kusuri o nomu under body. I limited body part + itai to atama and onaka.
6. Current entries cut for budget, each judged against a more common set in its topic: me ga sameru, doa ga aku, kagi ga kakaru, denki ga tsuku, heya ga chirakaru, toire o kariru, oto ga kikoeru, kakkou o suru, megane o hazusu, tebukuro o hameru, ka ni sasareru, hi ni yakeru, kuruma ni noseru, denpa ga hairu, suupu o nomu, koi koohii, kotoba ga tsuujiru, plus the pair members in note 4. newEntries.use: Mostly said without ga, about one in the forecast: shuumatsu taifuu kuru kamo (a typhoon might come this weekend). Taifuu kiteru means one has already come close and is nearby or heading in, not a forecast for later in the week; taifuu chikazuiteru stresses that it's getting closer, and taifuu kita means it has arrived. Often there's no verb at all: ashita taifuu da tte (they say there's a typhoon tomorrow).
newEntries.verbSense: come, arrive
newEntries.trap: English 'a typhoon hits' pushes to taifuu ga utsu or taifuu ga ataru, which don't work: with the typhoon as subject it just comes (taifuu kita). Ataru is fine the other way round, with your plans as subject and ni: ryokou ga taifuu ni atatchatta (our trip ran into a typhoon). Chokugeki (direct hit) is everyday talk too: toukyou chokugeki rashii yo (apparently it's heading straight for Tokyo); jouriku (landfall) mostly comes from the forecast.

example.ja: 明日台風来るらしいよ。
example.english: Apparently a typhoon's coming tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita taifuu ga kuru rashii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 明日台風が来るらしいですよ。
examplePolite.english: Apparently a typhoon's coming tomorrow.

newEntries.freqNote: 台風 is only #8171 because drama dialogue rarely turns to the weather; in typhoon season (roughly July to October) it is everywhere whenever one approaches, so commonness is a judgement. 来る is #52 (kana くる #429 is mostly -te kuru).
newEntries.notes: The cause takes de: taifuu de densha tomatta (the trains stopped because of the typhoon); once it's passed, taifuu sugita ne.

newEntries.use: About yourself it's a vague 'I'm off' (kyou chotto choushi warui). Put a body part or a device before no: onaka no choushi ga warui, sumaho no choushi ga warui (my phone's acting up). Ga often drops in casual talk, the opposite is choushi ii, and choushi dou? asks how things are going.
newEntries.verbSense: bad, in poor condition
newEntries.trap: A glitchy phone or PC isn't kowareta, which means it has stopped working (sumaho kowareta? is also said as an exaggeration). If it still works, just badly, it's choushi ga warui: sumaho no choushi warui.
partners: guai (condition: guai ga warui = feel unwell)
kaoiro (complexion: kaoiro ga warui = look pale)
me (eyes: me ga warui = poor eyesight)

newEntries.trap: Not furuku naru, which is for things: people take on years, toshi o toru, and 'I'm getting old' is the past, toshi totta.

newEntries.english: feel sick (queasy or faint); feel put off
newEntries.use: For feeling sick right now, in a crowd, a hot room or a car: chotto kibun ga warui (ga can drop, but it's kept far more than in kimochi warui), and kibun waruku natta when it comes on. Said about something someone did, it means it left you feeling put off: ano iikata, kibun warui.
newEntries.verbSense: bad
newEntries.trap: English 'I feel bad (about it)' is guilt, which is warui na or moushiwake nai, never kibun ga warui. Kibun ga warui is feeling sick, or feeling put off by something someone did; a grumpy mood that others can see is kigen ga warui.
partners: kigen (mood: kigen ga warui = be grumpy)
igokochi (comfort: igokochi ga warui = uncomfortable somewhere)

newEntries.notes: Kimochi warui is the queasier twin with a 'gross' sense; guai ga warui is general unwellness.

newEntries.use: Said of food, drinks, sleep and habits: yasai wa karada ni ii. The opposite karada ni warui is just as common (tabako, yofukashi), and since ii conjugates from yoi, the softer negative is karada ni yokunai. Ni is kept even in casual speech.
newEntries.verbSense: good; with ni, good for
newEntries.trap: Not kore wa kenkou desu: kenkou describes a person's health, so food or habits that are good for you are karada ni ii (kenkou ni ii also works). Kenkouteki na shokuji (a healthy diet) and herushii (light, healthy food) are fine too.

example.ja: 野菜も食べて。体にいいから。
example.english: Have some vegetables too. They're good for you.

examplePolite.romaji: yasai mo tabete kudasai. karada ni ii desu kara.
examplePolite.ja: 野菜も食べてください。体にいいですから。
examplePolite.english: Please have some vegetables too. They're good for you.

newEntries.freqNote: 体 (からだ) #371; いい #24; phrase entries 体にいい #11815 and 体に悪い #13606 (体に良い #44244); 健康 #2531.
newEntries.notes: Okarada ni ki o tsukete kudasai (take care of yourself) is the stock sign-off with karada; casually, karada ni ki o tsukete ne.

newEntries.use: Like onaka suita, said in the past for hunger you feel now: onaka hetta, with ga often dropped. It's a bit blunter and more casual than suita, and the rough, mostly male hara hetta is the form heard most in film. In desu/masu talk onaka ga sukimashita is the safer default; herimashita sounds blunt and a little male.
newEntries.verbSense: decrease, go down (taijuu ga heru = lose weight)
newEntries.trap: Hunger is a past-tense verb, not an adjective: onaka hetta (I'm hungry); onaka heru sounds like 'I'll get hungry'.
partners: hara (belly: hara hetta = rough, mostly male)

example.romaji: onaka hetta. nanka tabe ni ikanai?
example.ja: お腹減った。なんか食べに行かない？
example.english: I'm hungry. Want to go grab something to eat?

examplePolite.romaji: onaka ga herimashita ne. nanika tabe ni ikimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: お腹が減りましたね。何か食べに行きませんか？
examplePolite.english: I'm hungry, aren't you? Shall we go and get something to eat?

newEntries.freqNote: おなか #1253 (お腹 #4758); 減る #1173 counts every 'decrease' use. Phrase entry お腹が減る #60005, far below the rough 腹減った #4970 and 腹が減る #6497 (腹 #1216).
newEntries.notes: Same meaning as onaka ga suku, the one to say yourself; onaka hetta and its rough twin hara hetta are mainly forms to recognise when you hear them.

newEntries.use: For falling ill with something real (byouki ni natta), or as a warning about overdoing it. The ni always stays.
newEntries.verbSense: become, turn into
newEntries.trap: English 'I got sick' is usually something minor, but byouki ni natta sounds like a real illness: for a cold or a rough few days say kaze hiita, guai ga waruku natta or taichou kuzushita. Byouki desu ('I'm sick') sounds more serious still.

example.romaji: muri suru to byouki ni naru yo.
example.ja: 無理すると病気になるよ。
example.english: You'll make yourself sick if you push too hard.

examplePolite.romaji: kyonen, chichi ga byouki ni natte, shibaraku taihen datta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 去年、父が病気になって、しばらく大変だったんです。
examplePolite.english: My father got sick last year, and things were hard for a while.

newEntries.freqNote: 病気 #1019; なる #29 (成る #13300); phrase entry 病気になる #4880, high for a phrase.
newEntries.notes: Byouki ni kakaru (contract an illness) is more formal; getting better is byouki ga naoru.

newEntries.use: Heard as nuide (take them off) or nuida hou ga ii (you'd better take them off), and ofuku nuide (with the o- used to children) is what kids hear at bath time. When it's one layer, people name it: uwagi nuidara? (why not take your jacket off?). Casual speech drops o.
newEntries.verbSense: take off (clothes, shoes)
newEntries.trap: Not fuku o toru, which sounds like picking clothes up (fuku totte = pass me my clothes). Whatever goes on with kiru or haku (tops, trousers, shoes, socks) comes off with nugu. A hat comes off with toru or nugu. Glasses, masks, watches, ties and belts come off with hazusu, and casual toru works for most of them.

example.romaji: nureta fuku, hayaku nuida hou ga ii yo.
example.ja: 濡れた服、早く脱いだ方がいいよ。
example.english: You'd better get out of those wet clothes.

examplePolite.romaji: nureta fuku wa, hayaku nuida hou ga ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 濡れた服は、早く脱いだ方がいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: You'd better get out of those wet clothes.

newEntries.freqNote: Ranks are for 服 #1051 and 脱ぐ #2074. Pairing commonness is judged; in speech the garment is often named instead (上着 #6098).
newEntries.notes: Once it's clear which garment, nugu alone is enough: atsui kara nuijaou (it's hot, I'll take it off).

newEntries.use: Mostly heard as masuku hazushite (take your mask off) or hazushite mo ii? (OK if I take it off?). masuku hazushita kao (someone's face without the mask) comes up a lot too, as in masuku hazushita kao hajimete mita (first time I've seen your face without the mask). masuku hazushiteru means the mask is already off. Casual speech drops o.
newEntries.verbSense: remove, unfasten, detach
newEntries.trap: Not masuku o nugu for a face mask: nugu is for clothes and shoes. Masks, glasses, watches and rings come off with hazusu; casual toru (masuku totte) is just as everyday, though masuku totte can also mean 'pass me a mask'.

example.romaji: koko de masuku hazushite mo ii?
example.ja: ここでマスク外してもいい？
example.english: Is it OK to take my mask off here?

examplePolite.romaji: koko de masuku o hazushite mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: ここでマスクを外してもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: May I take my mask off here?

newEntries.freqNote: Ranks are for マスク #5039 and 外す #1043; 外す also counts 'miss' and 'step away' (seki o hazusu). マスク may be under-ranked if the drama corpus is mostly pre-2020. Pairing commonness is judged.
newEntries.notes: Putting one on is masuku o suru (or tsukeru). A mask pulled down under the chin is an ago masuku. A full-head costume or wrestler's mask is the one you nugu.

newEntries.use: For opening a door yourself or asking someone to: doa akete (open the door), often with kureru when your hands are full. Casual speech drops o; a door that is open is doa aiteru.
newEntries.verbSense: open something (a door, a box, your eyes)
newEntries.trap: English 'open' does both jobs. Someone opening it is akeru (doa akete); the door opening or being open is aku (doa aiteru).

example.ja: ごめん、ドア開けてくれる？
example.english: Sorry, can you open the door for me?

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, doa o akete moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: すみません、ドアを開けてもらえますか？
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, could you open the door?

newEntries.freqNote: 開ける #480 covers every kind of opening; the sound-alike 空ける (leave empty, make room) is #3596.
newEntries.notes: On the intercom, hai, ima akemasu ne (I'll let you in now) is a common reply when buzzing someone through the entrance; at your own front door it's usually hai, ima ikimasu.

newEntries.use: Mostly a request or reminder: doa shimete (shut the door), chanto shimete ne. Casual speech drops o; a door that is shut is doa shimatteru.
newEntries.verbSense: shut something (a door, a window, a lid); with kagi, lock
newEntries.trap: Not tojiru: dictionaries give it for 'close', but tojiru is for eyes, books and apps. Doors, windows and lids are shimeru.

example.ja: 寒いから、ドア閉めて。
example.english: It's cold, shut the door.

examplePolite.romaji: samui node, doa o shimete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 寒いので、ドアを閉めてください。
examplePolite.english: It's cold, so please close the door.

newEntries.freqNote: 閉める #1764; the sound-alike 締める (tighten, fasten) is #4630.
newEntries.notes: With kagi the same verb means lock: kagi shimeta? = did you lock up?

newEntries.use: The plain way to excuse yourself, usually with -te kuru since you'll be back: chotto toire itte kuru. Casual speech drops ni. toire itteru means someone has gone and is in there now (tanaka-san nara toire itteru yo), not that they're on the way. With strangers or at work, otearai ni itte kimasu sounds softer.
newEntries.verbSense: go
newEntries.trap: Not ofuro or basuruumu for 'bathroom': those mean the room you bathe in, which in most Japanese homes is separate from the toilet, so 'go to the bathroom' is toire ni iku.

example.ja: ちょっとトイレ行ってくる。
example.english: I'm just going to the bathroom.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto toire ni itte kimasu.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっとトイレに行ってきます。
examplePolite.english: I'll just go to the restroom.

newEntries.freqNote: お手洗い (otearai) #5898 is the politer word.
newEntries.notes: Asking where it is: toire doko? to friends, otearai wa doko desu ka? to staff.

newEntries.use: Usually an offer or a question: mado akete ii? (mind if I open the window?), mado akeyou ka. Casual speech drops o; a window that is open is mado aiteru.
newEntries.verbSense: open something (a door, a box, your eyes)
newEntries.trap: Not mado ga akete iru for 'the window's open': that is mado ga aiteru, or mado ga akete aru if someone left it open on purpose. akeru needs someone doing the opening (mado akete ii?).

example.ja: 暑いね、窓開けていい？
example.english: It's hot, mind if I open the window?

examplePolite.romaji: atsui desu ne, mado o akete mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 暑いですね、窓を開けてもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: It's hot, isn't it? May I open the window?

newEntries.freqNote: 開ける #480 also counts doors, boxes and eyes.
newEntries.notes: In a car, mado akete just means put the window down.

newEntries.use: Said when it turns cold or noisy or starts to rain: mado shimete (shut the window). Casual speech drops o; a shut window is mado shimatteru.
newEntries.verbSense: shut something (a door, a window, a lid); with kagi, lock
newEntries.trap: Not mado o shimaru: shimaru is the window closing or being shut (mado shimatteru); someone shutting it is shimeru (mado shimete).

example.ja: 雨降ってきた、窓閉めて！
example.english: It's started raining, shut the windows!

examplePolite.romaji: ame ga futte kita node, mado o shimete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 雨が降ってきたので、窓を閉めてください。
examplePolite.english: It's started to rain, so please close the windows.

newEntries.freqNote: The intransitive 閉まる (shimaru) is #3722.
newEntries.notes: mado shimeta? is a standard check before going out, alongside kagi kaketa?

newEntries.use: For setting off from home, usually saying or asking when: nanji ni uchi deru?, ima uchi deta (I've just left). Casual speech drops o; dekakeru (go out) is the single-verb alternative.
newEntries.verbSense: go out, leave; also come out, appear
newEntries.trap: English 'leave' leads to saru or hanareru, which sound like leaving for good (uchi o hanareru = leave home to live elsewhere); heading out for the day is deru: uchi o deru, and uchi kara deru is also fine.

example.ja: 何時にうち出る？
example.english: What time are you leaving the house?

examplePolite.romaji: nanji ni uchi o demasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 何時にうちを出ますか？
examplePolite.english: What time do you leave the house?

newEntries.freqNote: うち #113 also counts 内 'among/while'; 家 read いえ is #152. 出かける (dekakeru) is #1420.
newEntries.notes: Said with ie instead, ie o deru can mean moving out for good; iede is running away from home.

newEntries.use: Covers 'go home', 'come home' and 'get home': mou kaeru (I'm off home), uchi kaettara (once I'm home). uchi and ni are often dropped. mou kaetteru means they've already gone home, while ima kaetteru is casual for 'I'm on my way home' (also ima kaeri, kaeru tochuu).
newEntries.verbSense: go back to where you belong (home, your country)
newEntries.trap: Not uchi ni iku for going home yourself: iku is for going to someone else's place (tomodachi no uchi ni iku) or taking a friend along to yours (uchi iku?). Your own return home is kaeru, which also covers 'come home' and 'get home'.

example.ja: もううち帰った？
example.english: Are you home yet?

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa nanji goro uchi ni kaerimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今日は何時ごろうちに帰りますか？
examplePolite.english: Around what time are you going home today?

newEntries.freqNote: うち #113 also counts 内 'among/while'; 家 read いえ is #152.
newEntries.notes: Going back somewhere that isn't home (your desk, your seat) is modoru; for the office after a client visit, both kaisha ni modoru and kaisha ni kaeru are heard.

newEntries.use: Covers groceries as much as clothes: chotto kaimono itte kuru (I'm popping out to the shops). Casual speech drops ni. kaimono itteru means someone has gone shopping and is out now (okaasan nara kaimono itteru yo), not on the way; kaimono shiteru is being in the middle of shopping.
newEntries.verbSense: go (kaimono = kau 'buy' + mono 'things')
newEntries.trap: Not kaimono suru ni iku: the noun goes straight before ni iku (kaimono ni iku); with the verb it's the stem, kaimono shi ni iku.

example.ja: 買い物行くけど、なんかいる？
example.english: I'm going shopping, need anything?

examplePolite.romaji: kaimono ni ikimasu kedo, nanika irimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 買い物に行きますけど、何かいりますか？
examplePolite.english: I'm going shopping. Do you need anything?

newEntries.freqNote: Phrase not counted (the tokenizer splits it). The loanword ショッピング is #13644.
newEntries.notes: shoppingu (the loanword) leans to browsing malls for fun; kaimono covers any buying errand.

newEntries.use: Putting things back where they belong, as in the parent's nag heya katazukenasai. Casual speech drops o; vacuuming and wiping down is souji suru, and heya o kirei ni suru covers both.
newEntries.verbSense: put away, tidy; also clear (the table) or get (a job) done
newEntries.trap: 'Clean your room' points to souji suru, which is vacuuming, wiping and dusting; putting things away is katazukeru. Both are right, for different jobs.

example.ja: 今日は部屋片付けなきゃ。
example.english: I have to tidy my room today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa heya o katazukenakya ikenai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は部屋を片付けなきゃいけないんです。
examplePolite.english: I have to tidy my room today.

newEntries.freqNote: 片づける #2251 (片付ける #2543); 掃除 (souji) is #1393.
newEntries.notes: The mess it fixes is heya ga chirakaru (chirakatteru); a tidied room is katazuiteru.

newEntries.use: A daily chore in Japan, where most laundry is hung up to dry rather than tumble-dried: out on the balcony, or indoors (heyaboshi) when it rains. sentakumono hoshita? (did you hang the washing out?). Casual speech drops o.
newEntries.verbSense: hang out to dry; air in the sun
newEntries.trap: English 'hang' points to kakeru, but laundry put out to dry is hosu. The careful noun is sentakumono (the clothes); casual speech often shortens it to sentaku hosu.
partners: futon (futon: air it in the sun)

example.ja: 天気いいから、洗濯物干そう。
example.english: It's sunny, let's hang the washing out.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa tenki ga ii node, sentakumono o soto ni hoshimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は天気がいいので、洗濯物を外に干しました。
examplePolite.english: The weather's nice today, so I hung the laundry outside.

newEntries.freqNote: 洗濯 (sentaku, the washing itself) is #3221.
newEntries.notes: Bringing it in is torikomu (sentakumono torikonde!) and folding it is tatamu.

newEntries.use: For lifts, buses, ticket machines and intercoms: botan oshite (press the button), kono botan osu dake (you just press this button). Casual speech drops o; on a bus, pressing it asks for the next stop.
newEntries.verbSense: push, press

example.romaji: tsugi de oriru kara, botan oshite.
example.ja: 次で降りるから、ボタン押して。
example.english: We get off at the next stop, press the button.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, tsugi de orimasu node, botan o oshite moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: すみません、次で降りますので、ボタンを押してもらえますか？
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, I'm getting off at the next stop. Could you press the button?

newEntries.freqNote: 押す #1149 also covers pushing a door or a person.
newEntries.notes: Shirt buttons take other verbs: botan o tomeru (do up), hazusu (undo).

newEntries.use: Used to offer a cup and to talk about habits: koohii nomu? (want a coffee?), koohii wa nomanai (I don't drink coffee). Casual speech drops o, and koohii demo nomu? (a coffee or something?) softens an invitation.
newEntries.verbSense: drink; swallow without chewing

example.romaji: asa wa koohii nomanai to dame na n da.
example.ja: 朝はコーヒー飲まないとダメなんだ。
example.english: I can't get going in the morning without coffee.

examplePolite.romaji: asa wa koohii o nomanai to dame na n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 朝はコーヒーを飲まないとダメなんです。
examplePolite.english: I can't get going in the morning without coffee.

newEntries.freqNote: コーヒー #1154 (珈琲 #36261). 飲む #229 counts all drinking, medicine included.
newEntries.notes: To order, say koohii (o) onegaishimasu or koohii ni shimasu (I'll have coffee). Making it is koohii o ireru.

newEntries.use: Often heard as care and advice, after drinking alcohol or in the heat: mizu nonda? (have you had some water?), mizu nonde ne (make sure you drink water). Also when thirsty: nodo kawaita, mizu nomitai (I'm thirsty, I want some water). Casual speech drops o.
newEntries.verbSense: drink; swallow without chewing

example.romaji: atsui kara, mizu chanto nonde ne.
example.ja: 暑いから、水ちゃんと飲んでね。
example.english: It's hot, so make sure you drink enough water.

examplePolite.romaji: atsui node, omizu o chanto nonde kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 暑いので、お水をちゃんと飲んでくださいね。
examplePolite.english: It's hot, so please make sure you drink enough water.

newEntries.freqNote: 水 #797; the polite お水 (omizu) is counted separately (#3032). 飲む #229 counts all drinking.
newEntries.notes: mizu is cold or room-temperature water; hot water is oyu, not atsui mizu. In restaurants ask for omizu, which is free. In polite heat warnings you hear komame ni suibun o totte kudasai (keep taking fluids).

newEntries.use: Used to ask about and describe drinking: osake nomu? or osake nomeru? (do you drink?), anmari nomanai (I don't drink much). Casual speech drops o, and once drinking is the topic nomu alone means alcohol: kinou nomisugita (I drank too much last night).
newEntries.verbSense: drink; swallow without chewing
newEntries.trap: Learners take osake to mean Japanese sake, but it covers any alcohol, beer and wine included; rice wine is nihonshu.

example.romaji: kyou kuruma da kara, osake wa nomenai.
example.ja: 今日車だから、お酒は飲めない。
example.english: I'm driving today, so I can't drink.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa kuruma na node, osake wa nomenai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は車なので、お酒は飲めないんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm driving today, so I can't drink.

newEntries.freqNote: お酒 #1229; bare 酒 (sake) #1131 and ビール #1481 are counted separately. 飲む #229 counts all drinking.
newEntries.notes: nomi ni iku (go out for drinks) and nomikai (a drinking party) use the same nomu. How much you can take is osake ni tsuyoi / osake ni yowai, casually osake yowai n da (I'm a lightweight). Bare sake (sake nomou ze) is rougher, mostly male speech; osake is the everyday default for everyone.

newEntries.use: Said at home and at work, and as a soft offer or invitation: ocha demo nomu? (fancy a cup of tea?). Casual speech drops o, and ocha means whatever Japanese tea is on hand, including cold mugicha.
newEntries.verbSense: drink; swallow without chewing
newEntries.trap: English 'tea' means black tea, but ocha is green or other Japanese tea (mugicha, houjicha); black tea, with or without milk, is koucha.

example.romaji: chotto kyuukei shite, ocha demo nomou.
example.ja: ちょっと休憩して、お茶でも飲もう。
example.english: Let's take a short break and have some tea.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto kyuukei shite, ocha demo nomimashou.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと休憩して、お茶でも飲みましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's take a short break and have some tea.

newEntries.freqNote: お茶 #978 (bare 茶 #5292); 紅茶 (koucha) #5258 is counted separately. 飲む #229 counts all drinking.
newEntries.notes: ocha ni shiyou / ocha ni shimashou ka (let's stop for tea) is the usual way to call a tea break. ocha shinai? / ocha shiyou (go for tea) means a café break, coffee included. Making the tea is ocha o ireru.

newEntries.use: Said about any meal, not just rice. gohan tabeta? (have you eaten?) is a real question between family, partners and close friends, not a greeting as in Korean or Chinese; answer un, tabeta, or mada (tabetenai) for 'not yet', because tabenakatta means you skipped the meal. Casual speech drops o; the meal is named only when it matters (asagohan, ohiru, bangohan).
newEntries.verbSense: eat
newEntries.trap: Learners who know gohan as 'rice' avoid it for a pasta or burger dinner, but it is the everyday word for any meal (it means rice only when set against pan or men); shokuji (o) suru is stiffer.

example.ja: ご飯食べてから行くね。
example.english: I'll head over after I eat.

examplePolite.romaji: gohan o tabete kara ikimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: ご飯を食べてから行きますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll come over after I've eaten.

newEntries.freqNote: ご飯 #1225; kana ごはん #2244, the rough 飯 (meshi) #1398 and the stiffer 食事 (shokuji) #860 are counted separately. 食べる #130.
newEntries.notes: meshi kuu (meshi kutta?) is the rough, mostly male version.

newEntries.use: The everyday invitation: gohan ikou (let's get food) or kondo gohan ikanai? (want to get dinner sometime?), usually without ni in casual speech. Whether it means lunch or dinner comes from context.
newEntries.verbSense: go; with a purpose noun + ni, go out for it (kaimono ni iku)
newEntries.trap: English 'go out for dinner' pushes learners to spell it all out (yuushoku o tabe ni ikimasen ka, which is stiff) or to name the place (resutoran ni iku, which means a Western-style restaurant). Friends just say gohan ikou or gohan ikanai?, with no taberu; gohan tabe ni ikou also works.

example.ja: 仕事終わったら、ご飯行かない？
example.english: Want to grab dinner after work?

examplePolite.romaji: shigoto ga owattara, gohan ni ikimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: 仕事が終わったら、ご飯に行きませんか？
examplePolite.english: Would you like to go for dinner after work?

newEntries.freqNote: ご飯 #1225 (kana ごはん #2244 counted separately); 行く #40 counts all going. In the subtitles ni is dropped in nearly every case.
newEntries.notes: kondo gohan ikou ne is often a friendly 'let's get dinner sometime', not a fixed plan. At work the polite invitation is often shokuji ni ikimasen ka. For drinks it's nomi ni iku.

newEntries.english: the meal gets ready (dekita = it's ready)
newEntries.use: Called out from the kitchen: gohan dekita yo! (dinner's ready!), in the past tense and usually without ga. mou sugu dekiru yo (it's nearly ready) uses the non-past dekiru for what's coming.
newEntries.verbSense: come into being, get done; also 'can do' and 'be ready'
newEntries.trap: English 'dinner's ready' is in the present, but the kitchen call says the meal has come into being: gohan dekita yo; plain gohan dekiru yo means it'll be ready soon. The other everyday call is gohan da yo! (food's on!). If you reach for junbi, it's gohan no junbi (ga) dekita, the same dekiru as junbi dekita? (are you ready?).
partners: ryouri (a dish: ryouri dekita; ryouri dekiru? asks if you can cook)

example.ja: ご飯できたよ！早く来て。
example.english: Dinner's ready! Come quick.

examplePolite.romaji: gohan ga dekimashita yo. douzo, samenai uchi ni.
examplePolite.ja: ご飯ができましたよ。どうぞ、冷めないうちに。
examplePolite.english: Dinner's ready. Please, have it while it's hot.

newEntries.freqNote: ご飯 #1225 (kana ごはん #2244 counted separately). できる #73 is the kana form and pools every sense, mostly 'can do' (出来る #1313).
newEntries.notes: gohan dekiteru kara (the food's made) means it's already waiting for you. gohan yo! is the motherly, feminine version of gohan da yo. The rice cooker finishing is gohan ga taketa.

newEntries.use: Said about evenings and downtime, mostly as a habit or in the -teru form: terebi miteru (I'm watching TV), terebi miteta (I was watching TV), anmari terebi minai (I don't watch much TV). Casual speech drops o, and something you saw on TV is terebi de mita.
newEntries.verbSense: see, look at, watch

example.ja: 最近全然テレビ見ないな。
example.english: I don't watch TV at all these days.

examplePolite.romaji: saikin wa zenzen terebi o mimasen.
examplePolite.ja: 最近は全然テレビを見ません。
examplePolite.english: I don't watch TV at all these days.

newEntries.freqNote: verbRank is 見る pooling every sense (see, look, check); the shows-and-films spelling 観る is #10463.
newEntries.notes: On and off are terebi o tsukeru and terebi o kesu, as with denki; a show on TV is terebi de yatteru, a person terebi ni deteru.

newEntries.use: Said when you send or promise an email, with the person marked by ni: senpai ni meeru okutta (I emailed my senpai), ato de meeru okuru ne (I'll email you later). Sending something by email is meeru de okuru (shiryou meeru de okuru ne). Between friends, messages usually go by LINE: rain suru ne, rain okutta yo. Casual speech drops o.
newEntries.verbSense: send; see someone off

example.ja: 後でメール送るね。
example.english: I'll email you later.

examplePolite.romaji: ato de meeru o okurimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 後でメールを送りますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll email you later.

newEntries.freqNote: verbRank 送る also counts seeing someone off and sending parcels; 送信 (soushin, the 'send' button) is #6591.
newEntries.notes: The same okuru is seeing someone off or giving them a lift (eki made okuru); meeru suru is the shorter casual version.

newEntries.use: Said about listening habits and what you're listening to now, often in hobby talk (donna ongaku kiku?) and with nagara: ongaku kikinagara benkyou suru (study with music on). Casual speech drops o; putting music on for everyone is ongaku o kakeru.
newEntries.verbSense: listen, hear; ask
newEntries.trap: Not ongaku ni kiku: English 'listen to' has a 'to', but kiku takes o; kiku with ni means asking a person (sensei ni kiku).

example.ja: どんな音楽聞くの？
example.english: What kind of music do you listen to?

examplePolite.romaji: donna ongaku o kikimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: どんな音楽を聞きますか？
examplePolite.english: What kind of music do you listen to?

newEntries.freqNote: verbRank is 聞く pooling listen, hear and ask; the listening spelling 聴く is #1930.
alsoIn: vocab-trainer utility-vocab: school-subjects (ongaku, as a subject)
newEntries.notes: Music you happen to hear is ongaku ga kikoeru; music playing in a shop is ongaku ga kakatteru or nagareteru.

newEntries.use: Said about switching off a phone or other device, as an excuse (gomen, dengen kitteta = sorry, my phone was off) or a fix (ikkai dengen kitte mite). Cinema and exam announcements say keitai denwa no dengen o okiri kudasai. Casual speech drops o.
newEntries.verbSense: cut; cut off (a call, the power)
newEntries.trap: Not sumaho o kesu: powering a phone or device down is dengen o kiru ('cut the power'), with the device joined by no (sumaho no dengen kitte), or casually just keitai kitte; dengen o otosu is common too. Sumaho kesu can sound like turning only the screen off; kesu is for lights and the TV, though pasokon kesu is heard.

example.ja: 一回電源切ってみて。
example.english: Try turning it off for a moment.

examplePolite.romaji: ichido dengen o kitte mite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 一度電源を切ってみてください。
examplePolite.english: Please try turning it off for a moment.

newEntries.freqNote: Phrase entry 電源を切る is #16226 (the tokenizer merges only some uses); 電源を入れる is #32795.
newEntries.notes: On is dengen o ireru, and a phone that won't start is dengen ga hairanai (or tsukanai); one that shuts itself off is dengen kireta. Shutting down a computer is often dengen o otosu (pasokon otoshita). The kiru is the one in denwa o kiru.

newEntries.english: get in / ride in a car
newEntries.use: Covers getting in and riding along: kuruma notte (get in the car), kuruma nottara (once we're in). kuruma notteru is 'I'm in the car' (as in the example) and also 'drive / own one': donna kuruma notteru? (what car do you drive?). To say how you get there, use de: kuruma de iku.
newEntries.verbSense: ride; get onto (a vehicle, a bike, a ride)
newEntries.trap: Not kuruma ni hairu or kuruma o noru: getting in is ni noru (kuruma no naka ni hairu is only for ducking inside, say out of the rain). 'What car do you drive?' is kuruma nani notteru? or donna kuruma notteru?, while unten suru is the act of driving (unten dekiru? = can you drive?).

example.ja: 先に車乗ってるね。
example.english: I'll wait in the car.

examplePolite.romaji: saki ni kuruma ni nottemasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 先に車に乗ってますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll wait in the car.

newEntries.freqNote: No phrase entry. unten (driving) is #2725; asking what someone drives uses notteru.
newEntries.notes: Getting out is kuruma kara oriru; giving someone a ride is the transitive noseru: nosete kureru?

newEntries.use: Same frame as densha ni noru: basu notta (I've got on the bus, the usual text), basu notteru (I'm on the bus now), basu nottara (once I'm on), often chained as basu notte iku / kaeru. To say how you get there, use de: basu de iku. Casual speech drops ni.
newEntries.verbSense: ride; get onto (a vehicle, a bike, a ride)
newEntries.trap: Not basu o toru: 'take the bus' is ni noru, as with every vehicle.

example.ja: バス乗って帰ろうか。
example.english: Shall we take the bus home?

examplePolite.romaji: basu ni notte kaerimashou ka?
examplePolite.ja: バスに乗って帰りましょうか。
examplePolite.english: Shall we take the bus home?

newEntries.freqNote: No phrase entry. In film subtitles basu pairs with noru a third of the time.
newEntries.notes: On local buses you press the button for your stop (botan o osu); a bus that won't come is basu konai.

newEntries.use: The everyday word for parking, with ni for the spot: doko ni tomeru? (where shall we park?), koko tomete ii? (can I park here?). The same verb stops any car, so in a taxi you say koko de tomete kudasai.
newEntries.verbSense: stop (something moving); park (a car, a bike)
newEntries.trap: Not paaku suru (paakingu is a car park, as in koin paakingu) and not yameru (quit): parking is tomeru, 'stop' the car. chuusha suru is correct but formal, the word on signs (chuusha kinshi) and in polite asks; in everyday talk people still say chuushajou (car park) and chuusha ga nigate (I'm bad at parking).

example.ja: 車、どこに止めればいい？
example.english: Where should I park the car?

examplePolite.romaji: kuruma wa doko ni tomereba ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 車はどこに止めればいいですか？
examplePolite.english: Where should I park the car?

newEntries.freqNote: No phrase entry. 止める covers stopping anything, so its rank overstates the parking sense; the parking spelling 停める is #22793 and chuushajou (car park) #4816.
newEntries.notes: A car sitting there is the intransitive tomatteru: mise no mae ni kuruma tomatteru.

newEntries.english: get lost (wander off, like a lost child)
newEntries.use: Mostly about children who wander off (kodomo no koro, maigo ni natta koto aru = I got lost once as a kid) or a companion lost in a crowd. Adults say it of themselves half-jokingly, in a huge station or mall. For an adult who simply can't find the way, indoors or out, the default is mayotta (michi ni mayou). The ni usually stays.
newEntries.verbSense: become, turn into
newEntries.trap: Not maigo suru: maigo is a noun ('lost child'), so you become one, maigo ni natta.

example.romaji: hito ooi kara, maigo ni naranaide ne.
example.ja: 人多いから、迷子にならないでね。
example.english: There are lots of people, so don't get lost.

examplePolite.romaji: hito ga ooi node, maigo ni naranaide kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 人が多いので、迷子にならないでくださいね。
examplePolite.english: There are lots of people, so please don't get lost.

newEntries.freqNote: The whole phrase 迷子になる is listed at #7984, above 迷子 alone (#8524): the noun nearly always comes with naru (83% of its film uses). naru's rank covers every 'become'.
newEntries.notes: Getting separated from your group in a crowd is hagureru: tomodachi to hagurechatta.

newEntries.use: The usual way to talk about trips and plans: dokka ryokou iku? Casual speech drops the ni after ryokou, and a trip you're back from is ryokou itte kita. Going abroad is kaigai ryokou ni iku.
newEntries.verbSense: go
newEntries.trap: Not ryokou o toru ('take a trip'): you go on a trip, ryokou ni iku, or just ryokou suru.

example.ja: 夏休み、どっか旅行行かない？
example.english: Want to go on a trip somewhere over the summer break?

examplePolite.romaji: natsuyasumi, dokoka ryokou ni ikimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: 夏休み、どこか旅行に行きませんか？
examplePolite.english: Would you like to go on a trip somewhere over the summer break?

newEntries.freqNote: No phrase entry. tabi (#2626) is the more emotive 'journey', heard in set words (hitoritabi, tabi ni deru); plans and chat use ryokou.
newEntries.notes: A work trip is shutchou, not ryokou: ashita kara shutchou nan da.

newEntries.use: Heard in directions, mostly as the te-form request hidari ni magatte, often with the corner or light first, which takes o or de (tsugi no kado o / de hidari ni magatte). The side takes ni, sometimes e; migi ni magaru (turn right) works the same. In a taxi the verb often drops: tsugi, hidari de onegaishimasu.
newEntries.verbSense: bend; turn (when moving along a road)
newEntries.trap: Not hidari ni mawaru: mawaru is spin or go round; turning at a corner or light is magaru.

example.romaji: koko, hidari ni magaru n da yo ne?
example.ja: ここ、左に曲がるんだよね？
example.english: We turn left here, right?

examplePolite.romaji: koko o hidari ni magaru n desu yo ne?
examplePolite.ja: ここを左に曲がるんですよね？
examplePolite.english: We turn left here, don't we?

newEntries.freqNote: 左に曲がる is listed as a phrase at #25158 and 右に曲がる at #18193; migi is #1600. magaru (#3893) also covers bent things (nekutai magatteru).
newEntries.notes: Drivers and car navigation also say sasetsu / usetsu (left / right turn): koko usetsu dekinai yo (you can't turn right here).

newEntries.use: Mostly a phone or text update: ima eki tsuita (I'm at the station now), eki tsuitara renraku suru (I'll text when I get there). The past tsuita is how you say 'I'm here'; casual speech drops ni.
newEntries.verbSense: arrive; get to (a place)
newEntries.trap: eki ni touchaku suru is correct but stiff, the language of announcements and work emails; in conversation you arrive with tsuku, and 'I'm here' is the past tsuita.

example.romaji: eki tsuitara, kaisatsu no mae de matteru ne.
example.ja: 駅着いたら、改札の前で待ってるね。
example.english: When I get to the station, I'll wait in front of the ticket gates.

examplePolite.romaji: eki ni tsuitara, kaisatsu no mae de mattemasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 駅に着いたら、改札の前で待ってますね。
examplePolite.english: When I get to the station, I'll wait in front of the ticket gates.

newEntries.freqNote: No phrase entry. 着く is ranked apart from kana つく (#355), which mixes in the other tsuku verbs.
newEntries.notes: nanji ni tsuku? (what time do you get in?) and mou sugu tsuku (almost there) are the other everyday forms.

newEntries.use: Heard as konderu (busy now) or kondete (because it was busy), usually without ga: michi konderu kara okureru kamo. Plain komu is for patterns: kono jikan wa michi komu yo (the roads get busy at this hour). Same verb as mise ga komu and densha konderu. (sugoi konderu, with sugoi as an adverb, is casual; sugoku is the standard form.)
newEntries.verbSense: get crowded; konderu = be crowded, packed
newEntries.trap: Not michi ga isogashii: isogashii is for people and their time (isogashii hi, a busy day), never for a place full of people or cars. A busy road, train or shop is konderu ('has got packed').

example.ja: 今日、道すごい混んでるね。
example.english: The roads are really busy today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa michi ga sugoku kondemasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は道がすごく混んでますね。
examplePolite.english: The roads are really busy today.

newEntries.freqNote: No phrase entry. komu is written 混む or 込む, and the list splits them (#5984 / #10624). juutai (traffic jam) is #8673.
newEntries.notes: A full jam is juutai: juutai ni hamatta (I got stuck in traffic). Clear roads are suiteru: michi suiteta.

newEntries.english: be late for the train (and so miss it)
newEntries.use: Mostly said beforehand while rushing: densha ni okurechau! (I'll miss my train!), densha ni okurenai you ni (so we don't miss it). Keep the ni: with no particle, densha okureta is heard as the train running late, which is the usual excuse. Once it has gone, natives usually say noriokureta or nogashita: nebou shite densha noriokureta (I overslept and missed my train).
newEntries.verbSense: be late; fall behind time
newEntries.trap: Not densha o misu suru (misu is a mistake). And the particle flips it: densha ni okureru is you being late for it, densha ga okureru is the train running late.

example.romaji: sorosoro denai to, densha ni okurechau yo.
example.ja: そろそろ出ないと、電車に遅れちゃうよ。
example.english: We'd better head out soon or we'll miss the train.

examplePolite.romaji: sorosoro denai to, densha ni okuremasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: そろそろ出ないと、電車に遅れますよ。
examplePolite.english: We'd better head out soon or we'll miss the train.

newEntries.freqNote: No phrase entry. For a train that has already gone natives use noriokureru (#13876) and nogasu (#2510).
newEntries.notes: With a class or meeting the same frame just means late (jugyou ni okureta); a train doesn't wait, so late means missed.

newEntries.use: Said when you're in a hurry (mou jikan nai! = we're out of time) and as an excuse (ima jikan nai n da). Casual speech often drops ga. The past jikan nakatta and the -te form jikan nakute (no time, so...) are also common.
newEntries.verbSense: there isn't; not have (negative of aru)
newEntries.trap: Not jikan o mottenai: time exists or doesn't, so it's jikan ga nai.

example.romaji: gomen, ima chotto jikan nai n da.
example.ja: ごめん、今ちょっと時間ないんだ。
example.english: Sorry, I don't really have time right now.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, ima chotto jikan ga nai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、今ちょっと時間がないんです。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I don't really have time right now.

newEntries.freqNote: ない #43 is the kana form (無い #6807). The list has no phrase entry for 時間がない.
newEntries.notes: jikan aru? (got a minute?) is the question it answers; jikan ga aku (aiteru) is having a free slot. 'No time to cook' puts the verb first: ryouri suru jikan ga nai.

newEntries.use: The everyday 'I'm broke', usually okane nai in casual speech, often with ima or kongetsu. As a reason it's okane nai kara... (I'm broke, so...).
newEntries.verbSense: there isn't; not have (negative of aru)
newEntries.trap: okane mottenai is natural too, but it usually means no cash on you right now (ima okane mottenai), and about someone else, okane motteru means they're well-off. 'I'm broke' is plain okane nai, which can also mean no cash on you.
partners: genkin (cash: genkin nai = no cash on me)

example.ja: 今月、もうお金ない。
example.english: I'm already broke this month.

examplePolite.romaji: kongetsu wa mou okane ga nai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 今月はもうお金がないんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm already broke this month.

newEntries.freqNote: お金 #422; the blunter 金 (kane) is #670. ない #43 is the kana form (無い #6807).
newEntries.notes: kane nai, without o-, is blunter and mostly men's speech. For one purchase it's okane tarinai (not enough money).

newEntries.use: Asked before an invitation (shuumatsu yotei aru?) and given as the reason for saying no (sono hi wa chotto yotei aru n da). Casual speech drops ga, and yotei nai means 'I'm free'.
newEntries.verbSense: there is; have (things, events)
newEntries.trap: Not yotei o motteru: plans exist, so it's yotei ga aru. And 'got plans?' is yotei aru?, not keikaku aru?, which sounds like asking about a worked-out scheme (a project, a trip itinerary).

example.ja: 週末、なんか予定ある？
example.english: Got any plans for the weekend?

examplePolite.romaji: shuumatsu wa nanika yotei ga arimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 週末は何か予定がありますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you have any plans for the weekend?

newEntries.freqNote: 予定 #843; ある #21. No phrase entry. 計画 keikaku #1502 counts every sense of 'plan', including projects.
newEntries.notes: A booked plan is yotei haitteru. Drawing up a schedule (a trip, a study plan) is yotei o tateru; fixing a day with friends is hi o kimeru, and arranging to meet is yakusoku suru.

newEntries.use: For whether someone has paid, usually in the past: okane haratta? / mou haratta yo. When the amount, bill or method is said, okane drops: sen en haratta, kaado de harau.
newEntries.verbSense: pay; also brush or sweep off (dust, snow)
newEntries.trap: Paying back money you borrowed is kaesu (give back), not harau: ashita kaesu ne. When a friend covered your share, ato de harau ne works too.

example.ja: お金、もう払った？
example.english: Have you paid already?

examplePolite.romaji: okane, mou haraimashita?
examplePolite.ja: お金、もう払いました？
examplePolite.english: Have you paid already?

newEntries.freqNote: 払う #760. 支払う shiharau #2842 is the formal word used on bills and at the register.
newEntries.notes: Offering to pay is dasu (koko wa watashi ga dasu yo), and treating someone is ogoru. At the register staff ask oshiharai wa dou nasaimasu ka? (how will you pay?).

newEntries.english: not suit someone, can't make it (a time)
newEntries.use: For turning down a time: ashita tsugou warui (tomorrow's no good), or politely sumimasen, sono hi wa chotto tsugou ga warukute..., left trailing. Mostly for schedules; about a person it means 'doesn't suit them': jibun ni tsugou no warui koto wa kikanai (he won't listen to anything that doesn't suit him). With close friends, ashita chotto muri is also common.
newEntries.verbSense: bad, not good
newEntries.trap: English 'inconvenient' leads to fuben, which is for places and tools (eki kara tookute fuben = it's a pain, being so far from the station). A time that doesn't suit you is tsugou ga warui.
partners: taimingu (taimingu warui = bad timing, an unlucky moment; not a way to decline)

example.romaji: ashita tsugou warui kara, asatte wa?
example.ja: 明日都合悪いから、あさっては？
example.english: Tomorrow's no good for me. How about the day after?

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa chotto tsugou ga warui node, asatte wa dou desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 明日はちょっと都合が悪いので、あさってはどうですか？
examplePolite.english: Tomorrow doesn't really work for me. How about the day after?

newEntries.freqNote: Phrase entry 都合が悪い #16199. 不便 fuben #6936.
newEntries.notes: Often cut short to chotto tsugou ga..., with warui left unsaid.

newEntries.use: Said about the daily trip and about being a student at all, so you hear itteru a lot: nihongo gakkou itteru (I go to a Japanese language school). Casual speech drops ni, and e also works (gakkou e iku).
newEntries.verbSense: go
newEntries.trap: 'I'm going to school' (on the way) isn't gakkou ni itteru, which means you're there now or that you attend it. On the way is ima gakkou iku tochuu (or ima gakkou ni mukatteru), and about to leave is plain: ima kara gakkou iku.

example.ja: 最近日本語学校行ってる。
example.english: I've been going to a Japanese language school lately.

examplePolite.romaji: saikin nihongo gakkou ni ittemasu.
examplePolite.ja: 最近日本語学校に行ってます。
examplePolite.english: I've been going to a Japanese language school lately.

newEntries.freqNote: 学校 #661, 行く #40. No phrase entry. 通う kayou (attend regularly) is #1026.
newEntries.notes: For a regular routine, kayou also works: juku ni kayotteru.

newEntries.use: Said to open a question, usually with n da kedo, and here the ga mostly stays: shitsumon ga aru n da kedo. After nanika it's often dropped or becomes wa: teachers and presenters ask the room nanika shitsumon (wa) arimasu ka?
newEntries.verbSense: there is; have (things, plans, something to bring up)
newEntries.trap: English 'have' leads to motsu, but a question you have is aru: shitsumon ga aru. Asking it is shitsumon suru, or simply kiku.

example.romaji: hitotsu shitsumon ga aru n da kedo.
example.ja: 一つ質問があるんだけど。
example.english: I've got a question for you.

examplePolite.romaji: hitotsu shitsumon ga aru n desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: 一つ質問があるんですけど。
examplePolite.english: I've got a question for you.

newEntries.freqNote: 質問 #1058, ある #21. No phrase entry. 聞く kiku #67 is the everyday verb for asking.
newEntries.notes: To check before asking: shitsumon ii? (can I ask something?).

newEntries.use: Mostly heard about ability, in the potential: eigo hanaseru? (can you speak English?). With the potential, ga is as common as o: eigo ga hanaseru. Casual speech drops o. eigo de hanasu means talking in English at that moment: eigo de hanashite mo ii?
newEntries.verbSense: speak, talk; tell
newEntries.trap: 'Do you speak English?' is a plain present in English, but asking whether someone can takes the potential: eigo hanaseru? or eigo dekiru? Plain eigo hanasu? is understood, but it asks whether someone does speak it somewhere (ie de eigo hanasu no? = do you speak English at home?) or is about to, not whether they can.

example.ja: 英語はちょっとだけ話せる。
example.english: I can speak a little English.

examplePolite.romaji: eigo wa chotto dake hanasemasu.
examplePolite.ja: 英語はちょっとだけ話せます。
examplePolite.english: I can speak a little English.

newEntries.freqNote: 英語 #2574, 話す #151, potential 話せる #1219. しゃべる shaberu #745 is the casual twin (eigo shaberu). No phrase entry.
newEntries.notes: eigo dekiru? asks the same thing. Whether English gets you by somewhere is tsuujiru: eigo tsuujiru?

newEntries.use: Said while waiting on exam, medical or job-application results: kekka itsu deru? Once they're in it's kekka deta, and not yet is mada detenai. The ga is often kept.
newEntries.verbSense: go out; appear; come out (be announced or issued)
newEntries.trap: English 'I got my results' makes you the subject. For results being announced, Japanese says the results come out: kekka deta. kekka moratta only fits when a results sheet is handed to you (kenkou shindan no kekka moratta). kekka o dasu means producing results, at work or in sport.

example.ja: 試験の結果、もう出た？
example.english: Are your exam results out yet?

examplePolite.romaji: shiken no kekka wa mou demashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 試験の結果はもう出ましたか？
examplePolite.english: Have your exam results come out yet?

newEntries.freqNote: 結果 #626; 出る #81 counts every sense of deru. 結果を出す (produce results) has its own phrase entry at #8074; 結果が出る has none.
newEntries.notes: To ask how it went: kekka dou datta? (polite: kekka wa dou deshita ka?)

newEntries.use: Said by and to students, often as a reminder or a groan: shukudai shita? or shukudai shinakya (I've got to do my homework). The o is often dropped, and yaru is just as common: shukudai yatta?
newEntries.verbSense: do; the general verb for tasks

example.romaji: ato de issho ni shukudai shiyou.
example.ja: 後で一緒に宿題しよう。
example.english: Let's do our homework together later.

examplePolite.romaji: ato de issho ni shukudai o shimashou.
