examplePolite.english: Let's do our homework together later.

newEntries.freqNote: 宿題 #3935, する #15, やる yaru #45. In the subtitles 宿題 goes with する 28 times and やる 22 times, its two most frequent verbs (37% together). The counts are low only because 宿題 itself is rare in foreign-film subtitles.
newEntries.notes: Getting homework is shukudai ga deru (shukudai deta), and handing it in is dasu: shukudai dashita?

newEntries.use: Said about days off arranged with work, usually once they're booked: raishuu yasumi totta. The o is often dropped, and paid leave works the same way: yuukyuu totta. The everyday complaint is yasumi torenai (I can't get time off).
newEntries.verbSense: take; get (here: take time away from work, booked ahead or on the spot)
newEntries.trap: 'Take a break' for a few minutes isn't yasumi o toru, which on its own means time off, or rest in general (chanto yasumi totte ne, make sure you get some rest). For a few minutes, say chotto yasumou, kyuukei shiyou or kyuukei torou.

example.romaji: raishuu mikka yasumi totta n da.
example.ja: 来週三日休み取ったんだ。
example.english: I've booked three days off next week.

examplePolite.romaji: raishuu mikka yasumi o totta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 来週三日休みを取ったんです。
examplePolite.english: I've booked three days off next week.

newEntries.freqNote: 休み #1322, 取る #228 (撮る, take a photo, is counted separately at #649). 有給 yuukyuu #13555, 休暇 kyuuka #5687. No phrase entry. In the subtitles 休み + 取れる (can get time off) is the strongest pairing (log_dice 9.20).
newEntries.notes: A sick day is yasumu instead: kyou kaze de yasumu.

newEntries.use: Said about leaving a job for good, mostly as yameta (I quit) or as a complaint, yametai (I want to quit). Casual speech drops o, and shigoto o yameru means the same.
newEntries.verbSense: quit, leave (a job, school or club); same sound as yameru 'stop'
newEntries.trap: 'Leave the company' suggests kaisha o deru, but that normally means walking out of the office building (going home, heading out to lunch). Leaving the job is kaisha o yameru. Likewise daigaku o deru means graduating; dropping out is yameru.

example.ja: 去年会社辞めたんだ。
example.english: I quit my job last year.

examplePolite.romaji: kyonen kaisha o yameta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 去年会社を辞めたんです。
examplePolite.english: I quit my job last year.

newEntries.freqNote: The whole phrase 会社を辞める has its own entry in the drama list at #6363, and 仕事を辞める at #8598. 辞める #604 is the 'resign' spelling; kana やめる #117 mixes both senses.
newEntries.notes: Getting fired is kubi ni naru: kubi ni natta.

newEntries.use: Used for having a conversation, with to for the person and no for the topic: kare to sono hanashi shita (I talked to him about that), shigoto no hanashi shiteta (we were talking about work). X ni tsuite hanasu is fine too but sounds more structured. Casual speech drops o when hanashi has a word in front of it.
newEntries.verbSense: do; with a noun, carry out that activity (here, have a talk)
partners: uwasa (talking about someone who isn't there: X no uwasa shiteta = we were just talking about X)

example.ja: 何の話してたの？
example.english: What were you guys talking about?

examplePolite.romaji: nan no hanashi o shiteta n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 何の話をしてたんですか？
examplePolite.english: What were you talking about?

newEntries.freqNote: 話 #96 counts every hanashi use; する #15. Phrase entry 話をする #994.
newEntries.notes: nan no hanashi? on its own means 'what are you talking about?', when you're lost or denying something.

newEntries.english: listen to someone, hear someone out
newEntries.use: The everyday way to ask for or offer an ear: chotto hanashi kiite (just hear me out), hanashi kiku yo (I'm happy to listen). hito no hanashi kiitenai desho is the complaint 'you're not listening to me' (hito here means me, the speaker). It also covers hearing about something: sono hanashi kiita (I heard about that).
newEntries.verbSense: listen, hear; also ask
newEntries.trap: English 'listen to me' leads to watashi o kiite, but kiku takes what is said, not the person: watashi no hanashi kiite, or just chotto kiite. And kare ni kiku means ask him (or hear it from him), never listen to him.
partners: guchi (venting: guchi kiku yo = I'll hear you vent)
uwasa (rumour: sonna uwasa kiita = I heard a rumour like that)

example.ja: ちょっと、話聞いてよ。
example.english: Hey, just listen to me.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto hanashi o kiite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと話を聞いてください。
examplePolite.english: Please just hear me out.

newEntries.freqNote: 話 #96 counts every hanashi use; 聞く #67 (聴く #1930 separately).
newEntries.notes: X no iu koto o kiku = do what X says (oya no iu koto kikinasai).

newEntries.use: Among friends, the get-to-know-you question is kodomo iru? (got kids?), answered un, hitori iru. Politely you ask okosan imasu ka? (or okosan wa irasshaimasu ka?), answered futari imasu. The number goes after the noun: kodomo futari iru (I have two kids). kyoudai iru? and kanojo iru? work the same way.
newEntries.verbSense: be, exist (people and animals); with ga, have (people, pets)
newEntries.trap: English 'have' leads to kodomo o motte iru or the thing-verb aru; in talk, kids, siblings and partners take iru: kodomo iru?, kyoudai iru? (kodomo o motsu oya, parents with children, is written style).

example.romaji: uchi wa kodomo futari iru n da.
example.ja: うちは子供二人いるんだ。
example.english: We've got two kids.

examplePolite.romaji: uchi wa kodomo ga futari iru n desu.
examplePolite.ja: うちは子供が二人いるんです。
examplePolite.english: We have two children.

newEntries.freqNote: 子供 #589 (子ども #2264 separate spelling); kana いる #42 merges the -te iru auxiliary (居る #6802).
newEntries.notes: kodomo dekita = we're having a baby, or we've had kids (kekkon shite kodomo mo dekita).

newEntries.use: Opens a serious or personal talk and usually trails off with n da kedo: chotto hanashi ga aru n da kedo... Natives usually keep the ga here, though chotto hanashi aru n da kedo is heard too. Politely it's hanashi ga aru n desu kedo, and to a boss or client often ohanashi ga aru n desu ga.
newEntries.verbSense: there is; have (things, plans, something to bring up)
newEntries.trap: English 'I need to talk to you' leads to hanasu hitsuyou ga aru, which sounds stiff and official; the everyday opener is chotto hanashi ga aru n da kedo.
partners: youji (something to see to: kimi ni youji ga aru = I need you for something)

example.romaji: chotto hanashi ga aru n da kedo, ima ii?
example.ja: ちょっと話があるんだけど、今いい？
example.english: I need to talk to you. Got a minute?

examplePolite.romaji: chotto ohanashi ga aru n desu kedo, ima ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: ちょっとお話があるんですけど、今いいですか？
examplePolite.english: There's something I'd like to discuss. Do you have a moment?

newEntries.freqNote: 話 #96 counts every hanashi use; お話 #654 (the polite ohanashi); ある #21. No phrase entry.
newEntries.notes: ii hanashi ga aru n da kedo = I've got a good offer for you (a classic sales opener). Plain good news is more often ii shirase.

newEntries.use: Heard mostly as a rebuke: monku iwanaide (stop complaining), monku bakkari (always complaining). Complaining to a shop or a neighbour is also monku o iu, and being on the receiving end is monku iwareta (someone complained to me). Casual speech often drops o.
newEntries.verbSense: say
newEntries.trap: English has one verb, 'complain'; Japanese says the complaint: monku o iu, not monku suru. Dictionary picks sound formal: kujou o iu is lodging a complaint with a landlord or company, fuhei o iu is bookish, and kureemu (from 'claim') is a customer complaint to a business. Venting about your day is guchi o iu.

example.ja: 文句ばっかり言わないでよ。
example.english: Stop complaining all the time.

examplePolite.romaji: monku bakari iwanaide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 文句ばかり言わないでください。
examplePolite.english: Please stop complaining so much.

newEntries.freqNote: 文句 #1359; 言う #28. Phrase entry 文句を言う #7153.
newEntries.notes: monku aru? (got a problem with that?) is the confrontational retort, and monku nai yo (no complaints, fine by me) the easy-going reply; both belong to monku ga aru.

newEntries.use: For talking about thanking rather than doing it (arigatou does that): orei iwanakya (I have to thank them), chanto orei itta? (did you thank them properly?), orei iitakute (I wanted to say thanks).
newEntries.verbSense: say
newEntries.trap: English 'thank' leads to kansha suru, which is being grateful (kansha shiteru = I'm grateful), not saying it: 'I have to thank them' is orei iwanakya. orei o suru means giving something back, like a gift or a meal.
partners: oiwai (congratulations: oiwai iitakute = I wanted to congratulate them)

example.ja: 後でちゃんとお礼言わなきゃ。
example.english: I need to thank them properly later.

examplePolite.romaji: ato de chanto orei o iwanakya ikemasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: 後でちゃんとお礼を言わなきゃいけませんね。
examplePolite.english: I really should thank them properly later.

newEntries.freqNote: お礼 #968; bare 礼 #3119, so the o- form is the spoken headword. 言う #28.
newEntries.notes: orei ni = as thanks: orei ni gohan ogoru yo (dinner's on me, as thanks).

newEntries.use: Said by the one being treated. When someone offers to pay (kyou wa ogoru yo), you accept with jaa, gochisou ni narimasu, and afterwards you thank them with gochisou ni narimashita, to a boss, senpai or host. Among friends gochisousama! does both jobs, and telling someone about it is gochisou ni natta or, more often, ogotte moratta (they paid for me).
newEntries.verbSense: become; here, come to be the one treated
newEntries.trap: English 'I got treated' leads to the passive gochisou sareta, which is heard but less usual; people say gochisou ni natta (like osewa ni naru), ogotte moratta or ogorareta. The payer's verbs are ogoru and gochisou suru.
partners: yakkai (imposing: tomodachi no ie ni yakkai ni naru = stay at a friend's place)

example.romaji: kinou senpai ni gochisou ni natta.
example.ja: 昨日先輩にごちそうになった。
example.english: My senpai treated me to a meal yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou wa gochisou ni narimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日はごちそうになりました。
examplePolite.english: Thank you for dinner yesterday.

newEntries.freqNote: ごちそう #2702 (kana; ご馳走 #15229); ごちそうさま #2052 is its own entry. naru: kana なる #29. Phrase entry ごちそうになる #6670 (ご馳走になる #43407).
newEntries.notes: gochisou on its own is a feast or treat: sugoi gochisou (what a spread).

newEntries.use: Two everyday uses: growing up over the years (otona ni nattara = when you're grown up) and acting mature: otona ni natta ne (you've really grown up), motto otona ni natte yo (grow up a bit).
newEntries.verbSense: become (with ni after a noun)
newEntries.trap: English 'grow up' leads to sodatsu, which is being raised or growing as a child (toukyou de sodatta = I grew up in Tokyo); becoming an adult, or acting like one, is otona ni naru.

example.ja: 大人になったら分かるよ。
example.english: You'll understand when you're older.

examplePolite.romaji: otona ni nattara wakarimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 大人になったら分かりますよ。
examplePolite.english: You'll understand when you're older.

newEntries.freqNote: 大人 #898; naru: kana なる #29. Phrase entry 大人になる #1753, high for a phrase.
newEntries.notes: otonappoi = mature for your age; otonagenai = childish (of an adult). To a child, 'when you grow up' is usually ookiku nattara (ookiku nattara nani ni naritai?).

newEntries.use: Said about reading as a habit or right now: hon toka yomu? asks if someone reads, and hon yonderu is 'is reading' (or, with mainichi, 'reads every day'). Casual speech drops o, as in hon yomu no suki (I like reading).
newEntries.verbSense: read, silently or aloud

example.ja: 最近なんか面白い本読んだ？
example.english: Read any good books lately?

examplePolite.romaji: saikin nanika omoshiroi hon o yomimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 最近何か面白い本を読みましたか？
examplePolite.english: Have you read any good books lately?

newEntries.freqNote: manga 漫画 #3363 and zasshi 雑誌 #2341 take the same yomu.
newEntries.notes: Reading named as a hobby is dokusho (shumi wa dokusho desu); in chat, hon yomu no ga suki sounds more natural.

newEntries.use: Said about films at home or at the cinema, often without o in casual speech (eiga miru). 'Have you seen it yet?' is the past tense mou mita?, and 'have you ever seen it?' is mita koto aru?
newEntries.verbSense: see, look at, watch
newEntries.trap: 'Not yet' is mada mitenai, not mada minai, which means 'I'm not going to watch it yet'.

example.ja: あの映画、もう見た？
example.english: Have you seen that movie yet?

examplePolite.romaji: ano eiga, mou mimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: あの映画、もう見ましたか？
examplePolite.english: Have you seen that movie yet?

newEntries.freqNote: 観る, a spelling often used for films and shows, is ranked separately at #10463; it is the same miru.
newEntries.notes: The invitation is eiga mi ni ikanai? or just eiga ikanai?: eiga mi ni iku and plain eiga ni iku both mean go to the movies.

newEntries.use: utau already means sing, so uta is often dropped when the song is obvious, as in karaoke de nani utau? (what'll you sing at karaoke?). The full uta (o) utau is for singing in general: uta utau no suki (I like singing).
newEntries.verbSense: sing

example.romaji: ofuro de uta utau no suki.
example.ja: お風呂で歌うたうの好き。
example.english: I like singing in the bath.

examplePolite.romaji: ofuro de uta o utau no ga suki desu.
examplePolite.ja: お風呂で歌を歌うのが好きです。
examplePolite.english: I like singing in the bath.

newEntries.freqNote: 曲 (kyoku, a particular song or track) #2119 takes the same utau: kono kyoku utaeru?
newEntries.notes: Praise usually names uta: uta umai ne! (casual) or uta ga ojouzu desu ne (polite), both meaning 'you're a great singer'. utau no umai ne is also fine.

newEntries.use: Said about securing tickets for concerts, games, flights or the shinkansen, often ones that sell out. You hear the can-form toreru most, which takes ga (usually dropped in speech): chiketto toreta! (got them!), torenakatta (couldn't get any).
newEntries.verbSense: take; also get hold of, secure (seats, bookings, rooms)
newEntries.trap: Not chiketto o morau, which means someone gave them to you: tickets you secure yourself are toru (kau, buy, is also fine), and 'I got them!' is toreta! (casually also getto shita!).

example.ja: ライブのチケット取れた！
example.english: I got tickets for the concert!

examplePolite.romaji: raibu no chiketto ga toremashita!
examplePolite.ja: ライブのチケットが取れました！
examplePolite.english: I got tickets for the concert!

newEntries.freqNote: 取れる (toreru, the toreta form) is ranked on its own at #631. Films say chiketto o kau (48) far more than toru (9): kau is the plain everyday pairing, and toru lives in Japanese booking talk about hard-to-get tickets, which subtitles under-count. 切符 (kippu) #11210 is far rarer than chiketto.
newEntries.notes: kippu is a train ticket (kippu o kau); for the shinkansen you hear both. chiketto covers concerts, games, flights and anything booked online.

newEntries.english: understand what something means; (negative) make no sense
newEntries.use: Mostly heard in the negative as a casual reaction, with ga dropped: imi wakannai (that makes no sense) about a rule, a joke or someone acting strangely. Aimed at what someone just said, it's blunt, close to 'you're not making sense'; with someone above you, ask dou iu imi desu ka? instead. imi wakaru? (you get what I mean?) checks that someone is following you.
newEntries.verbSense: understand, be clear; here the meaning gets through to you
newEntries.trap: For 'that makes no sense', learners say imi ga nai, but imi nai means 'it's pointless' (yatte mo imi nai). Something that doesn't add up is imi wakannai: you can't get the meaning. wake wakannai and the slangy imifu say the same.

example.ja: 何それ、意味分かんない。
example.english: What? That makes no sense.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, chotto imi ga yoku wakaranai n desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、ちょっと意味がよく分からないんですけど。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I don't quite follow what you mean.

newEntries.freqNote: The list has no entry for 意味が分かる or 意味分かんない, since the tokenizer splits them; the contraction 分かんない alone is #1567.
newEntries.notes: For 'oh, that makes sense', the usual reply is naruhodo; aa, imi wakatta means 'oh, now I get it'.

newEntries.english: be in a good mood; feel well
newEntries.use: About your mood, usually with ga dropped: kyou kibun ii (I'm in a good mood today). It also covers feeling well again after feeling sick: kibun yoku natta? (feeling better?). After a shower or a walk, sukkiri shita is more usual.
newEntries.verbSense: good, fine; here your mood is good
newEntries.trap: English 'feel good' covers everything, but kimochi ii is how something feels to you (a bath, a breeze, finally finishing), while kibun ii is your mood or how you feel overall. The negative isn't the mirror: kibun warui means feel sick, or feel put off (sonna koto iwarete kibun warui). Someone else being grumpy is kigen ga warui (kachou kigen warui); for yourself, iraira shiteru (I'm irritable) is more usual.
partners: choushi (condition: choushi ga ii, doing well)

example.romaji: kyou wa nanka kibun ii n da.
example.ja: 今日はなんか気分いいんだ。
example.english: I'm in a good mood today for some reason.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa nanka kibun ga ii n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はなんか気分がいいんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm in a good mood today for some reason.

newEntries.freqNote: The phrase entry 気分がいい is #13225; the tokenizer usually splits it, and the ga-less 気分いい has no entry.
newEntries.notes: ii kibun (a nice feeling) is common too: nanka ii kibun. gokigen da ne means 'you're in a good mood'.

newEntries.use: The everyday empathy line, with ga dropped: sono kimochi wakaru (I know how you feel), often flipped as wakaru, sono kimochi. With wa it sets up a 'but': kimochi wa wakaru kedo... (I get it, but...), the gentle way to disagree.
newEntries.verbSense: understand; here, relate to how someone feels
newEntries.trap: For 'I know how you feel', learners say kimochi o shitteru, but shiru is knowing a fact: kimi no kimochi shitteru means 'I know what your feelings are' (say, a crush). Relating to someone is wakaru: sono kimochi wakaru.

example.ja: 分かる分かる、その気持ち。
example.english: Oh, I totally know how you feel.

examplePolite.romaji: sono kimochi, yoku wakarimasu.
examplePolite.ja: その気持ち、よく分かります。
examplePolite.english: I know exactly how you feel.

newEntries.freqNote: The list has no entry for the whole phrase, so the noun and verb are ranked separately. In the subtitles wa (261 of 437) outnumbers ga (105), as in kimochi wa wakaru kedo.
newEntries.notes: hito no kimochi ga wakannai (has no idea how other people feel) is a common complaint about someone tactless. To a customer or someone senior it's okimochi: okimochi wa wakarimasu ga... (I understand, but...).

newEntries.use: Nearly always in -te ru for how you feel now: tanoshimi ni shiteru (I'm looking forward to it). The thing takes o, often dropped: ryokou tanoshimi ni shiteru. Polite tanoshimi ni shitemasu closes many messages and plans.
newEntries.verbSense: do, make; with X ni, make something into X (here, a pleasure ahead), not the 'go with' of kore ni suru
newEntries.trap: English 'look forward to' has no matching verb, and 'I can't wait' as matenai sounds like you've run out of patience. Say tanoshimi ni shiteru or just tanoshimi!; machikirenai (can't wait) is also fine.

example.romaji: jaa, raishuu tanoshimi ni shiteru ne.
example.ja: じゃあ、来週楽しみにしてるね。
example.english: Okay, looking forward to next week!

examplePolite.romaji: jaa, raishuu tanoshimi ni shitemasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: じゃあ、来週楽しみにしてますね。
examplePolite.english: Well then, I'm looking forward to next week.

newEntries.freqNote: The phrase has its own entry, 楽しみにする #1435, high for a phrase; suru's #15 covers every use of suru.
newEntries.notes: tanoshimi ni shitete ne (look forward to it!) is what you say when you've planned a surprise.

newEntries.use: Said about a place or a group you feel at ease in, usually without ga: kono kafe igokochi ii. It also works for people: kare to iru to igokochi ii (I feel at ease with him).
newEntries.verbSense: good, nice; here being there feels good
newEntries.trap: For a place or people you feel at ease with, learners reach for kaiteki (comfortable), which is physical comfort and sounds like an ad; say igokochi ii. Don't stretch it to objects: a comfy chair is raku or suwarigokochi ii, comfy shoes are hakiyasui.

example.romaji: kono mise, nanka igokochi ii yo ne.
example.ja: この店、なんか居心地いいよね。
example.english: There's something really cosy about this place.

examplePolite.romaji: kono mise, igokochi ga ii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: この店、居心地がいいですね。
examplePolite.english: This place is so cosy, isn't it?

newEntries.freqNote: The bare noun ranks low because it almost only occurs in this phrase, which has entries of its own: 居心地がいい #18169, 居心地いい #22077.
newEntries.notes: The opposite, igokochi warui, means you feel awkward or out of place.

newEntries.english: have no motivation, can't be bothered
newEntries.use: About yourself it's the flat 'I just don't feel like it': kyou yaruki nai (I just don't feel like doing anything today). About someone else it's a criticism, they're not trying: ano hito yaruki nai yo ne. In polite talk people usually say yaruki nai desu or yaruki ga nai n desu; yaruki ga arimasen sounds stiff.
newEntries.verbSense: nai: there isn't, have none (negative of aru)

example.romaji: kyou maji yaruki nai. nanimo shitakunai.
example.ja: 今日マジやる気ない。何もしたくない。
example.english: I've got zero motivation today. I don't want to do anything.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa nanka yaruki nai n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はなんかやる気ないんですよ。
examplePolite.english: I just don't feel like doing anything today.

newEntries.freqNote: The list has no entry for the whole phrase; ない #43 (無い #6807).
newEntries.notes: yaruki denai is 'I can't get going'; yaruki nai is flatter: I just don't feel like it, or, about others, they don't care.

newEntries.use: Said when luck goes someone's way: un ii ne! (lucky you), with ga dropped. The past un yokatta (that was lucky) is just as common. Ii becomes yo- in its other forms, so it's never un iikatta.
newEntries.verbSense: ii: good (past yokatta)
newEntries.trap: English 'lucky' is an adjective on the person. Japanese usually makes luck the subject, un ga ii (your luck is good), though rakkii! and tsuiteru are just as natural in casual speech. 'Good luck!' before a test or game is ganbatte, not anything with un.
partners: engi (engi ga ii: a good omen)

example.romaji: ichiban mae no seki? un ii ne!
example.ja: 一番前の席？運いいね！
example.english: Front-row seats? Lucky you!

examplePolite.romaji: ichiban mae no seki desu ka? un ga ii desu ne!
examplePolite.ja: 一番前の席ですか？運がいいですね！
examplePolite.english: Front-row seats? You're lucky!

newEntries.freqNote: 運 #4015 (kana うん #49 is mostly 'yeah'); いい #24. The phrase has its own entries: 運がいい #11653, 運が良い #16963. ラッキー #2636; ツイてる #8862; 幸運 kouun #4863.
newEntries.notes: Un ii ne (lucky you) sounds the same as un, ii ne (yeah, nice), so context decides. Kouun (幸運) is the written word.

newEntries.use: The verdict on someone's manner, a shop's staff or a place: ano ten'in-san, kanji ii ne, with ga dropped. Before a noun, ga often becomes no: kanji no ii hito (a pleasant person). The opposite, kanji warui (rude, off-putting), is at least as common.
newEntries.verbSense: ii: good
newEntries.trap: English 'nice' pulls toward yasashii, but yasashii is a kind, gentle nature. The pleasant impression a person's manner or a place gives is kanji ga ii, and yasashii is wrong for a place. Rude or off-putting is kanji warui.
partners: inshou (inshou ga ii: make a good impression)
fun'iki (fun'iki ga ii: a nice atmosphere)

example.romaji: ano mise no ten'in-san, kanji ii ne.
example.ja: あの店の店員さん、感じいいね。
example.english: The staff at that shop are so pleasant.

examplePolite.romaji: ano mise no ten'in-san wa kanji ga ii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの店の店員さんは感じがいいですね。
examplePolite.english: The staff at that shop are very pleasant.

newEntries.freqNote: 感じ #305, though much of that is ii kanji and tte kanji; いい #24. いい感じ has its own entry at #1668 and the opposite 感じ悪い is #8684, but 感じがいい / 感じいい are not listed. The film count (441) is mostly ii kanji (ADJ:410), so commonness is judged.
newEntries.notes: In the reverse order, ii kanji (いい感じ) means 'going well, looking good': ii kanji da ne! Kanji (感じ, feeling) sounds the same as kanji (Chinese characters).

newEntries.english: be capable, good at one's job
newEntries.use: Praise for a capable coworker, usually shigoto dekiru (ga dropped), or before a noun, where ga often becomes no: shigoto ga dekiru hito / shigoto no dekiru hito (someone good at their job). Dekiru alone can carry it (dekiru hito da ne), and shigoto ga dekinai is blunt criticism. It's said about someone: telling a superior to their face that they're capable sounds presumptuous.
newEntries.verbSense: dekiru: can do; here, be capable, perform well
newEntries.trap: Not shigoto ga jouzu. Jouzu praises how skilfully something is done (e ga jouzu, ryouri ga jouzu), while dekiru says someone is capable. Being good at your job is shigoto ga dekiru, usually as shigoto ga dekiru hito.
partners: benkyou (benkyou ga dekiru: do well at school)
undou (undou ga dekiru: be good at sports, athletic)

example.romaji: atarashii buchou, sugoku shigoto dekiru n da yo.
example.ja: 新しい部長、すごく仕事できるんだよ。
example.english: The new manager's really good at her job.

examplePolite.romaji: atarashii buchou wa totemo shigoto ga dekiru kata na n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 新しい部長はとても仕事ができる方なんですよ。
examplePolite.english: Our new manager is extremely capable.

newEntries.freqNote: 仕事 #134; できる #73 (出来る #1313). No phrase entry. 優秀 yuushuu #1364; 有能 yuunou #7229; 上手 jouzu #1309.
newEntries.notes: Outside of praise it's literal: ashita shigoto dekinai (I can't work tomorrow). Yuushuu (excellent) is the formal word.

newEntries.english: have good taste, a good eye
newEntries.use: A stock compliment on clothes, a gift, a room or a playlist: sensu ii ne! Ga is usually dropped. The opposite is sensu nai (no taste), and sensu ga aru means a flair for something (ryouri no sensu ga aru).
newEntries.verbSense: ii: good
newEntries.trap: 'Good taste' isn't aji (flavour). Sensu is a false friend: sensu nai means 'no taste', not 'that doesn't make sense' (imi wakannai). 'That makes sense' is naruhodo, and common sense is joushiki.

example.ja: その服、センスいいね。
example.english: Great taste, that outfit.

examplePolite.romaji: sono fuku, sensu ga ii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: その服、センスがいいですね。
examplePolite.english: That outfit shows great taste.

newEntries.freqNote: センス #2690; いい #24. No phrase entry; 趣味がいい #53080; おしゃれ #3483. The film count (17) is too low to use, so commonness is judged.
newEntries.notes: Shumi ga ii also means good taste, but shumi mostly means 'hobby', and ii shumi shiteru ne is often sarcastic.

newEntries.use: The plain way to say someone is a good, kind person: ano hito, seikaku ii yo ne, with ga dropped. Before a noun it's seikaku no ii hito, and it often pairs with looks: kao mo ii shi seikaku mo ii. Seikaku warui (mean, nasty) is harsh and common in gossip.
newEntries.verbSense: ii: good
newEntries.trap: Not ii seikaku: in that order, ii seikaku shiteru ne is usually sarcastic ('you've got some nerve'). The compliment keeps seikaku first: seikaku ii, seikaku no ii hito. Seikaku warui is far stronger than 'not nice': it means mean or nasty.
partners: sutairu (sutairu ga ii: have a good figure)

example.romaji: ano hito, honto ni seikaku ii yo ne.
example.ja: あの人、ほんとに性格いいよね。
example.english: She's such a nice person, isn't she?

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito wa hontou ni seikaku ga ii desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの人は本当に性格がいいですよね。
examplePolite.english: She really is a lovely person, isn't she?

newEntries.freqNote: 性格 #1670; いい #24. The negative is much more frequent in dramas: 性格悪い #14102 and 性格が悪い #30468, against 性格がいい #47898. 人柄 hitogara #7228.
newEntries.notes: Ii hito also means 'a nice person', but ii hito na n da kedo... is the classic brush-off (nice, but not for me).

newEntries.use: Said about your own bad luck (kyou un warui naa) or to console someone: un warukatta ne (that was just bad luck). Casual speech drops ga.
newEntries.verbSense: warui: bad
newEntries.trap: As with un ga ii, luck is the subject: un ga warui (my luck is bad). For your own bad day, tsuitenai is the more natural casual choice (kyou tsuitenai naa); un warukatta ne is the usual consolation.
partners: engi (engi ga warui: a bad omen)

example.ja: 今日、ほんと運悪いなあ。
example.english: I'm having such bad luck today.

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa un ga warukatta desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: それは運が悪かったですね。
examplePolite.english: That was just bad luck.

blocks.label: Rain and snow
blocks.rationale: What rain and snow do and what you do about it: it's coming down, it has stopped, the umbrella's own verb, and getting rained on.
blocks.interference: ame ga furu and yuki ga furu share furu, so drill them in one frame (soto, ___ futteru yo). ame ni furareta (it rained on me) is the same furu in its suffering passive, so set it against plain ame futta. Keep ame ga yamu (it stops by itself) apart from yameru (a person quits), and kasa o sasu (have it up) apart from kasa motsu (carry it).

blocks.label: Weather small talk
blocks.rationale: The remarks people trade about conditions outside: nice weather, strong wind, heavy rain, a breeze, a typhoon on the way, and how early it gets dark.
blocks.interference: kaze ga tsuyoi and ame ga tsuyoi both use tsuyoi where English says 'windy' and 'heavy', so learn them in one frame (kyou ___ tsuyoi ne). kaze (wind) sounds exactly like kaze (a cold), and only the verb tells them apart: kaze ga fuku / kaze ga tsuyoi vs kaze o hiku. A typhoon just kuru (comes) rather than 'hits', and the kureru in hi ga kureru is not kureru 'give'.

blocks.label: Hungry, full, thirsty
blocks.rationale: Everyday appetite signals: hungry (two ways), full and thirsty.
blocks.interference: onaka suita and onaka hetta mean the same, but hetta sounds blunter, so learn suita first and hetta as its casual twin. Both use the past tense for hunger you feel now, and so does nodo kawaita. onaka ippai has no verb of its own (add ni natta for the past).

blocks.label: Aches and injuries
blocks.rationale: Saying what hurts: X ga itai for pain, plus stiffness and injury.
blocks.interference: X ga itai is pain (atama itai, onaka itai). kata ga koru is stiffness and takes the verb koru, never itai. kega o suru is the injury itself with suru, and the hurt part takes o (ashi kega shita).

blocks.label: Feeling unwell
blocks.rationale: Feeling off and what you do about it: see a doctor, take medicine, lie down.
blocks.interference: guai ga warui is feeling unwell in general, choushi ga warui is being off form (or a machine acting up), and kibun ga warui is feeling sick or faint right now. kimochi warui (in senses) is queasy or gross. yoko ni naru is lying down to rest, not neru (sleep). English 'take' and 'see' pull toward toru and miru, but medicine takes nomu and a doctor visit is byouin ni iku.

blocks.label: Getting sick
blocks.rationale: Coming down with something: a cold, a fever, catching it from someone, falling ill.
blocks.interference: kaze o hiku is getting a cold; kaze ga utsuru is catching it from someone. netsu ga aru is having a fever now; netsu ga deru is it coming on (netsu deta). byouki ni naru is a real illness, so a cold is kaze hiita, not byouki ni natta. kaze 'cold' sounds like kaze 'wind' (kaze ga fuku).

blocks.label: Everyday body
blocks.rationale: Body sets outside illness: what's good for you, getting older, sweat and haircuts.
blocks.interference: These verbs sound like others. The kiru in kami o kiru means cut (kitta), not wear (fuku o kiru, kita). The kaku in ase o kaku is not write or draw (e o kaku). Getting older is toshi o toru, not furuku naru. karada ni ii (good for you) is not kimochi ii (feels good).

textFixes.value: Onaka hetta (onaka ga heru) means the same but sounds a little blunter; hara hetta is the rough, mostly male version. Onaka pekopeko (I'm starving) sounds childish or cute.

The sets next to it split the job. Choushi ga warui is being off form, and also a machine acting up (pasokon no choushi ga warui). Kibun ga warui is feeling sick or faint right now (in a car, in a crowd). Kimochi warui (in the senses list) is queasy, but also 'gross, creepy'.
Giving your cold to someone else is kaze o utsusu: kaze utsushichatta, gomen (sorry, I gave you my cold).

blocks.label: Clothes and shoes
blocks.rationale: The everyday on/off talk for what you're dressed in: clothes and shoes go on, shoes come off at the door, clothes come off, trousers go on like shoes.
blocks.interference: kiru vs haku: kiru for the torso or whole body (shirt, coat, dress), haku for anything you step into (shoes, socks, trousers, skirts); nugu takes all of them off, so drill kiru/haku against the one nugu (kutsu haite / kutsu nuide).

blocks.label: Masks, hats and glasses
blocks.rationale: Things worn on the head and face, each with its own verb, plus hazusu for taking a mask (or glasses) off.
blocks.interference: Three verbs for 'wear': masuku o suru (small items), boushi o kaburu (pulled over the head), megane o kakeru (hung on the ears). Masks and glasses come off with hazusu, never nugu; a hat comes off with toru or nugu.

blocks.label: Out and back
blocks.rationale: Leaving the house, locking up, running errands and getting home: the trip that starts and ends every day.
blocks.interference: The particle shows direction: o for the place you leave (uchi o deru), ni for where you end up or what you go to do (uchi ni kaeru, kaimono ni iku). 'Go home' is kaeru, because uchi ni iku means visiting someone's house.

blocks.label: Bathroom
blocks.rationale: The washroom routine people mention morning and night: the toilet, a shower, a bath, teeth.
blocks.interference: shawaa o abiru and ofuro ni hairu are both 'take a ___' in English, but a shower is poured over you (o abiru) and a bath is gone into (ni hairu). Drill them in one frame: saki ni ___ kuru ne.

blocks.label: Doors and windows
blocks.rationale: Opening and closing around the house: one verb pair for both doors and windows, then the door that is open or opens by itself.
blocks.interference: akeru and shimeru need someone doing it, with o. ga + aku is what the door does or how it is now, so keep doa akete (open it) apart from doa aiteru (it's open).

blocks.label: Lights and buttons
blocks.rationale: Switching things on and off and pressing a button: the on/off pair plus the press.
blocks.interference: Don't carry akeru and shimeru over from doors: lights go on with tsukeru and off with kesu (not shimeru or tomeru). Drill the pair in one frame: denki ___te.

blocks.label: Housework and pets
blocks.rationale: Home life that comes up in small talk: trash day, tidying, laundry, having a pet.
blocks.interference: Each verb beats the English pick: gomi o dasu, not suteru, for collection day; katazukeru (put away), not souji (scrub); hosu (hang to dry), not kakeru. The kau in inu o kau sounds like kau 'buy'.

blocks.label: Sleep and waking
blocks.rationale: Bedtime to morning: dreaming, waking up, setting the alarm.
blocks.interference: okiru from the versatility list gets mixed up with me ga sameru. okiru can mean getting out of bed, but me ga sameru never does: you can wake at 4 and not get up until 7.

textFixes.value: suitchi o ireru / dengen o ireru is how you switch a machine on; eakon o ireru is also heard, but tsukeru is the everyday choice. Intransitive pair: denki ga tsuku, mostly heard as denki tsuiteru (the light's on) and denki tsukanai (it won't come on). denki tsukete ends like ki o tsukete (take care), the same verb in another sense.
Unlocking is kagi o akeru. The locked state is kagi ga kakaru, nearly always heard as kagi kakatteru (it's locked); kagi shimatteru is just as common.

blocks.label: Drinks
blocks.rationale: Water, coffee, alcohol and tea all take nomu, and ocha o ireru is making the tea or coffee in the first place.
blocks.interference: All four share nomu, so drill them in one frame (mizu nomu? koohii nomu?), and kusuri o nomu in Body uses the same verb. ocha o ireru is making the tea, not drinking it, and it is never ocha o tsukuru.

blocks.label: Meals at home
blocks.rationale: Saying dinner's ready, eating, and the two everyday comments on how food tastes.
blocks.interference: gohan means the meal here, not only rice: gohan dekita yo means it's ready, and gohan tabeyou means let's eat. A taste you notice uses suru (hen na aji suru), not aru. Bland is aji ga usui, never yowai; yowai belongs to osake ga yowai.

blocks.label: Eating and drinking out
blocks.rationale: An evening out: suggesting a meal, finding the place packed, asking to smoke, and saying you're a lightweight.
blocks.interference: gohan ni iku needs no taberu. mise ga komu is said as konderu (a verb) and is not mise ga aiteru (open). Tobacco takes suu, not the nomu of drinks. osake ga yowai is about the drinker, while kono osake tsuyoi means the drink is strong.

blocks.label: TV, music, photos
blocks.rationale: What you do with screens and sound in your free time: watch TV, listen to music, take photos, sit on your phone, put music on.
blocks.interference: ongaku o kiku (you listen) vs ongaku o kakeru (you put it on): same noun, different job, so drill them as a pair (nani kiiteru? / ongaku kakete ii?). English 'play' is never asobu here, and terebi miteru and sumaho miteru share miru while ijiru is the fiddling verb.

blocks.label: Phone calls
blocks.rationale: One phone call on the noun denwa: calling out, picking up, hanging up, a call coming in.
blocks.interference: denwa o kakeru (you call) vs denwa ga kakaru (a call comes in): o vs ga, plus kara for the caller, show the direction; with the caller as subject, add -te kuru: okaasan ga denwa kakete kita. kiru ends the call and is not a form of kakeru.

blocks.label: Messages
blocks.rationale: A message's round trip: you send one, one comes in, you reply.
blocks.interference: meeru o okuru (you send, o) vs meeru ga kuru (it comes to you, ga): the same out/in split as denwa o kakeru / denwa ga kakaru. kaesu 'send back' sounds like kaeru 'go home', so learn it with its object.

blocks.label: Battery, power, Wi-Fi
blocks.rationale: When a phone stops working or gets switched off, mostly said in the negative or the past as a complaint or excuse.
blocks.interference: dengen o kiru (you switch it off) vs juuden ga kireru (it runs out by itself): transitive kiru and intransitive kireru, the same pair as denwa o kiru / denwa ga kireta. Lights and the TV take kesu, not dengen o kiru.

textFixes.value: meeru now means email; a text from a friend is a rain (LINE): rain kita. henji and renraku work the same way: henji kita. Sending is meeru o okuru: okutta yo (I sent it).
nagasu (let flow) is the alternative in shops and at events: biijiiemu o nagasu. Listening is ongaku o kiku; kakeru only starts it playing.
Charging is the plain verb juuden suru. The same kireru is a dropped call: denwa kireta (the call cut off). Switching the phone off yourself is dengen o kiru, the transitive half.
Intransitive pair: denki ga kieru (the light goes out; denki kieta! = the lights went out). A phone or computer is powered off with dengen o kiru.

blocks.label: Getting on and off
blocks.rationale: The ride itself: one frame, X ni noru, for train, bus and car, then oriru to get off and a free seat once you're aboard.
blocks.interference: Getting on takes ni and getting off takes o (densha ni noru, densha o oriru), so drill them as a pair, and 'take the bus' is never toru. seki ga aiteru means one seat is free; a whole empty train is densha ga suiteru.

blocks.label: On the way
blocks.rationale: The texts you send on your way to meet someone: I'm at the station, the train's late, will I make it, the roads are jammed, I missed it.
blocks.interference: densha ga okureru (the train is late) and densha ni okureru (you were late for it, so you missed it) differ only in ga or ni. Keep the train as the subject in densha okureteru, and say densha ni okureta or nogashita for missing it. Crowded roads are konderu, never isogashii.

blocks.label: Trips and errands
blocks.rationale: Heading out for a reason: a trip, picking someone up, stopping in on the way, and parking when you get there.
blocks.interference: konbini ni yoru (drop in) gets mixed up with tomaru (a car pulls up, or you stay the night) and with kuruma o tomeru (park). yoru is the visit and tomeru is what you do with the car. In mukae ni iku, Japanese says iku where English says 'I'll come'.

blocks.label: Finding the way
blocks.rationale: Directions, and losing your way: turning at the corner, losing the route, getting separated from your group.
blocks.interference: michi ni mayou (you can't find the route) and maigo ni naru (you've got separated, like a lost child) both come out as 'get lost'. Tie mayou to the route and maigo to the person who has gone missing. Turning is magaru, not mawaru (spin).

textFixes.value: norikaeru (change trains) is a single verb. The transitive is noseru, giving someone a ride: nosete kureru? (can you give me a lift?)

Heard as okureteru (it's running late) or okurete (because it was late), as in gomen, densha okurete... Casual speech drops ga, so densha okureta means the train was late. Swap ga for ni and you are the one who was late: densha ni okureta (I missed the train).

Mostly heard as a check or a result: maniau? (will we make it?), maniatta (made it), maniawanai (we won't make it). The noun drops once the train is clear. Once it has gone, say densha ni okureta, or more casually nogashita or noriokureta (I missed it), above all shuuden nogashita (I missed the last train).

The place you got lost in takes de: eki no naka de mayotta. Getting separated from the people you're with, like a child in a shop, is maigo ni naru. Asking the way is michi o kiku: sumimasen, chotto michi o kikitai n desu kedo.

Not konbini ni tomaru: that tomaru is a car pulling up there (konbini de tomatte = pull over at the konbini; parking is kuruma o tomeru), and the overnight tomaru never fits a shop. Dropping in on the way is yoru: konbini yotteku.

blocks.label: Time and getting ready
blocks.rationale: Hurrying and how long things take: no time, are you ready, it takes a while, time going by.
blocks.interference: kakaru vs tatsu: ichinen kakatta = it took a year, ichinen tatta = a year has gone by. Readiness is asked in the past (junbi dekita?), never junbi dekiru?.

blocks.label: Costs and paying
blocks.rationale: Money in everyday talk: being broke, what something costs overall, one item's price, paying, and splitting the bill.
blocks.interference: Three verbs for English 'cost' and 'pay': okane ga kakaru is the overall cost (kekkou kakatta), ikura suru is an item's price (ikura shita?), okane o harau is you handing it over. warikan ni suru is splitting evenly, not wakeru. okane nai uses the same nai frame as jikan nai.

blocks.label: Are you free?
blocks.rationale: One conversation about setting a time: are you free, have you got plans, does it suit, and the polite ways to say no.
blocks.interference: aiteru (got a gap) vs yotei aru (got plans) is the yes/no; tsugou ii / warui is the tactful pair for whether a time suits. yotei ga aru is just having plans, yotei haitteru says the day is already booked, youji ga atte is the vague errand excuse; something 'comes up' as youji ga dekita or yotei ga haitta.

blocks.label: Errands and saving
blocks.rationale: Running errands and budgeting: grab some cash, is the shop open yet, save up, nothing to spare.
blocks.interference: A shop's aiteru means 'open', not 'free' as in ashita aiteru?. orosu (take out) and tameru (save up) both take okane o. yoyuu ga nai is having no slack in money, time or headspace; okane ga nai is simply broke.

textFixes.value: 'Something came up' is kyuu ni youji ga dekita or kyuu ni yotei ga haitta, not okita (that sounds like an accident). Plain 'I have plans' is yotei ga aru, never yotei o motteru; haitteru adds that the day is already taken.
Paying for someone is ogoru (kyou wa ogoru yo = it's on me); being treated is gochisou ni naru.

blocks.label: School and learning
blocks.rationale: Everyday school talk, guessable sets first: going to school, homework, having a question, speaking English, then the thanks phrase benkyou ni naru.
blocks.interference: shitsumon ga aru (have a question) is not shitsumon suru (ask one), and benkyou ni natta (I learned from it) is not benkyou shita (I studied). eigo o hanasu means you can speak English; eigo de hanasu means you talk in English.

blocks.label: Work and time off
blocks.rationale: The working week from smallest break to biggest: clocking off, missing a day, booking leave, quitting.
blocks.interference: yasumu and yameru sound alike: shigoto o yasumu is a day off, kaisha o yameru is for good. shigoto o yasumu is missing work (often sick, short notice), while yasumi o toru is leave you book.

blocks.label: Exams and results
blocks.rationale: An exam from start to finish: you sit it, the results come out, you pass or fail.
blocks.interference: ukeru (take, with o) and ukaru (pass, with ni) sound alike, and ochiru is ukaru's opposite. Results come out with ga (kekka ga deru); kekka o dasu means getting results yourself.

blocks.label: Talking to people
blocks.rationale: The everyday talk sets: talking, hearing someone out, opening a serious chat, going up to someone, and staying in touch.
blocks.interference: hanashi o suru (you talk), hanashi o kiku (you listen, or do what someone says) and hanashi ga aru (I need to talk to you) all share hanashi, so drill them together. koe o kakeru (go up to someone, give them a shout) is not hanasu, and renraku o toru (stay in touch, manage to reach someone) is not the one-off renraku suru from the versatility list.

blocks.label: Friends and family
blocks.rationale: The people in your life: making friends, being close, having kids, growing up.
blocks.interference: dekiru is the moment something starts and iru is having it: tomodachi dekita (made a friend) and kodomo dekita (we're expecting), against tomodachi iru? and kodomo iru? (got friends? got kids?). otona ni naru (become an adult) is not sodatsu (be raised) or ookiku naru (get bigger).

blocks.label: Lies, jokes and complaints
blocks.rationale: What friends say to each other: lies, jokes, complaints and secrets.
blocks.interference: Lying takes tsuku (uso tsuita), but joking and complaining take iu (joudan itta, monku iwanaide). uso da yo and joudan da yo both mean 'just kidding'. naisho takes ni suru, not mamoru.

blocks.label: Favours, sorry, cheer up
blocks.rationale: Asking a favour, apologising for the trouble or worry you caused, and cheering someone up.
blocks.interference: onegai ga aru is asking a favour and onegai o kiku is granting one. meiwaku o kakeru and shinpai o kakeru put trouble or worry on someone else, while shinpai suru means you are the one worrying. genki dashite (cheer up) is not ganbatte (hang in there).

blocks.label: Guests and thanks
blocks.rationale: Thanking people, plus the host-and-guest lines: say thanks, don't go to any trouble, thanks for having me, thanks for the meal.
blocks.interference: In osewa ni naru and gochisou ni naru, ni naru puts you on the receiving end; the giver says sewa o suru, or gochisou suru / ogoru. ki o tsukau (fuss over others) is not ki o tsukeru (be careful) or ki ni suru (mind).

textFixes.value: Wanting friends is usually tomodachi hoshii or tomodachi tsukuritai. Having them takes ga iru, as in kodomo ga iru: dekita is the moment it happens, iru is having them (tomodachi iru?).
gochisou ni naru (be treated to a meal) is built the same way: with ni naru, you are the one receiving.

blocks.label: Feels good or bad
blocks.rationale: How something feels to you: a sensation in your body (kimochi), your mood (kibun), or a place or group you're in (igokochi).
blocks.interference: English 'feel good' covers all three. kimochi ii is a physical sensation (a bath, a breeze), kibun ii is your mood or feeling well, and igokochi ii is a place you like being in. kimochi warui means queasy or gross, not ill: being ill is guai ga warui.

blocks.label: Noticing and understanding
blocks.rationale: Perceiving and understanding: a smell or a sound 'does' (ga suru), you notice something (ki ga tsuku), and you get what it means or how someone feels (wakaru).
blocks.interference: The smell or sound is the subject (nioi suru, oto shita), so you don't use kagu or kiku. ki ga tsuku (notice) sounds almost like ki o tsukeru (be careful). imi wakaru is about meaning and kimochi wakaru is about feelings; both use wakaru, never shitteru.

blocks.label: Likes and interests
blocks.rationale: How you feel about a thing or a plan: you like it (ki ni iru), you're into it (kyoumi ga aru), you can't wait for it (tanoshimi ni suru).
blocks.interference: ki ni itta (I love it) sounds like ki ni natta (it bugged me). ki ni iru is for something you have or have tried, kyoumi ga aru is for wanting to know more, and tanoshimi ni shiteru is for something still ahead.

blocks.rationale: Your energy and mood: no motivation, getting yourself going, getting hyped, stress piling up.
blocks.interference: yaruki nai is a flat state and is also said about other people; yaruki denai means you can't get yourself going. Mood goes up (tenshon agaru) while stress piles up (tamaru). tenshon means hype, not tension (that's kinchou).

consistency.notes:
I checked contrast groups against the chunk-stage groups, because merge.py applies those over the entry and fix values. Example: the chunker renamed denki o tsukeru / kesu to tsukeru-kesu and moved doa ga aku into akeru-shimeru. These fixes are keyed by slug, so they apply after the chunk groups.

(1) Duplicates: there are none, so nothing is dropped. onaka ga suku / onaka ga heru and michi ni mayou / maigo ni naru are synonyms, not the same set, and all four are common. michi ni mayou / maigo ni naru already have different English glosses. onaka ga heru had the same gloss as onaka ga suku ('get hungry') in the same block and group, so it now says it is the blunter, casual one. Its notes called onaka hetta mostly something to recognise, which contradicts its own use line and how common it is to say, so that is rewritten.

(2) Spelling: koohii, eakon, konbini, juuden and the joined -teru/-chau/-toku forms are the same everywhere. There were two departures from kotoba's convention, which the versatility list confirms: 'kocchi' in hidari ni magaru partners (should be kotchi) and 'janai' in joudan o iu use (should be ja nai, copula separate). Both are fixed. honto (casual) next to hontou (polite examples) is deliberate and matches the versatility item 'honto ni'.

(3) Groups: two groups had only one member after chunking. dengen o kiru still had the old name denki-tsuku-tsukeru, so it joins tsukeru-kesu with denki o tsukeru / kesu. mise ga komu sat alone in komu-crowded while michi ga komu had no group; they are now paired. Open/close, wear/take-off, noru/oriru, okureru/maniau, ukaru/ochiru, takai/hikui and un ii/warui all already share groups. I left the ii/warui feeling sets split (kimochi/kibun/igokochi ga ii in feel-good, against guai/choushi/kibun/kimochi ga warui) because they split by meaning, not by mistake. jikan ga tatsu sits in take-verbs even though it isn't a 'take' set. Its trap contrasts it with jikan ga kakaru, so I left it.

(4) englishVerb: three values carried qualifiers or lists. kasa o sasu ('put up / open') becomes open, the word its trap (akeru) comes from. me ga warui ('have (bad eyes)') becomes have. ocha o nomu ('have, drink') becomes have. Separately, michi ga komu said 'get crowded', but its trap is about 'busy' (isogashii), so it becomes busy. I left multi-word phrasal values without qualifiers as they are (take off, keep in touch, need to talk).
